FOREWORD This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Leather, Tanning Materials and Allied Products Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. The leather industry occupies a privileged an expanding export market for finished order to facilitate unambiguous exchange inculcate an increasing scientific bias in published in 1960. position in the trade table of this country. Of late, the development of leather goods has further heightened the interest in this industry. In of commercial and scientific information within the industry, and to the use of terms, current in the leather trade, the standard was first

In the preparation of this glossary, most of the indigenous terms in use in the Indian hides, skins and leather trade, together with their synonyms and common terms in vogue, have been included. The glossm-y, however, limits itself strictly to terms related to hides, skins and leather; terms relating to footwear and other trades, general, chemical and Other terms pertaining to proprietary and patented items being not included. Terms which may be commonly used in the leather industry but convey commonly accepted dictionary meanings have been excluded. [n this revision, additional terms have been added and a few terms which have lost significance have been deleted, It is hoped that this glossary will prove useful to the leather trade in general and the Indian leather industry in particular. The composition of the Committee for formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. include all

This standard is intended chiefly to cover the technical definitions of terms. and it may not necessarily the legal implications of the terms.

GLOSSARY OF TERMS RELATING TO HIDES, SKINS AND LEATHER
(First Revision )
1 SCOPE This standard defines the terms strictly relating to hides, skins and in the Indian leather trade and industry. 2 TERMINOLOGY A A --Abbreviation used by exporters of hides to denote the following descriptions of hides -- Agras, Assortment. Thus, a bale of hides marked A denotes the Assortment Agra. Aarhat -- Warehouses or godowns for hides and skins where dealers bring hides and skins for sale. There are several such godowns in centres like Agra, Amritsar, Calcutta, Delhi, Julhmdur, Kanpur, etc, and they constitute what are known as hide markets. The buyers, chietly exporters and tanners come to these aar%ats to make their purchases. Aarhatdar-- The proprietor of an aai-hat, who acts as a commission and selling agent for the beparis. Usually he finances the beparis by advancing him the value of a consignment against railway receipt and he is responsible for the safe keeping of goods until sold. The aarhatdar negotiates terms and prices with the buyers and the beparis are not usually allowed to interfere. For this service, the aarhatdar charges a commission from the bepari. Aarhatdari -- The commission that a bepari has to pay to an aarhatdar when his goods are sold. Abrasion Resistance -- The reciprocal of the loss in thickness of leather after a definite amount of abrasive action on it. An important property of sole leather. Abyssinia Hides -- Abyssinian cattle are of the zebu type with a definite hump. The raw hide is usually washed to give `bathed' hides. The chief cwntre of the trade is the town ofAddis Ababa, from which is derived the common trade description of all Abyssinian hides as `Addis Ababa Bathed' or `Addis Ababa Unbathed'. Acid Bate -- Bates that can be used in thepH range of 3-5; active even at 20"C; smoothens the grain; less drastic than alkaline bates; can be used on chromed stock also after an acid wash to remove the free chrome in the leather. 1 Acid Number -- The quantity of base, expressed in milligrams of potassium hydroxide that is required to neutralize the acid constituents present in one gram of oil, fat, wax and fatty acid. Acid Salt Ratio -- The ratio of acids and total neutral salt present in the tanning material or its extract, both being expressed in terms of milliequivalent per 100 g of air dried material. It is a measure of astringency of a vegetable tanning material. Acid Soaking -- Soaking with the addition of acid to accelerate the process in respect of hides and skins cured by drying. Acidity -- In the leather trade, the term represents the acid content of the liquor (tan liquor) which is expressed in terms of milligram equivalent per litre. Actually, acidity represents the hydrogen ion (H+) or hydronium ion (H30+) concentration and as the degree of dissociation for different acids varies, acidity is generally expressed in terms ofpH value. The term is also used for referring to the acidity of tanned leathers. Acrylic Syntan -- Essentially a polymer of acrylic and/or methacrylic acid with a small amount of an agent like sodium alginate incorporated into the polymer. Acorn Cup -- See CValonia'. Activated Sludge Process --A biological wastewater treatment process in which a mixture of wastewater and activated sludge is agitated and aerated. The activated sludge is subsequently separated from the treated wastewater by sedimentation or returned to the process as need may be. Ageing -- Keeping or resting in a heap or pile for a certain time with a view to maturing or seasoning. Aggregation -- The dyestuffs and vegetable tannins form addition compound but the degree of aggregation depends largely on ionic groups present. This to an extent controls the dyeing of leathers. Acid Colours -- Group of aniline dyes which are compounds of organic acids and an inorganic base, usually sodium hydroxide. A strong acid, such as sulphuric or formic acid, has to be added to the dye bath in order to liberate the organic acids which are responsible for the dyeing (see also `Dye `).

IS 1640:2007 Agras -- These are well-cleaned dry-cured hides of good leather substance, the flesh side of which is yellowish in colour (see also `Jullunders' and `A'). Air-Dried Hides -- Hides cured by exposure of the flesh side to mild rays of the sun until they are dry. Airing Off -- Slightly drying the stock (leather) after application of finish. Airless Spray -- Spraying instead of compressed air. with hydraulic pressure Alum Tanning or Tannage -- A technique of preparing leather solely with a mixture the essential active ingredient of which is an aluminium salt, often, but not ecessarily alum, for example, alum, salt, egg yolk and flour. The natural colour of the leather is white (see also `Tawing Paste'). Ammunition Leather -- Vegetable, chrome and combination tanned leather curried and finished for making military boots (see `Army Grain' and `Russet'), Amphoteric Syntan -- Aliphatic amines condensed with novolaks using Mannich reaction in organic solvents. The products are soluble in water though there are no sulfonic groups and are amphoteric in character. Amritsars -- A variety of goatskins now collected from Punjab and Rajasthan. On account of their large spread, they are sought-after for upholstery and carriage work. Angle of Weave -- See `Weave, Angle of'. Angular Spray -- Spraying of finishes at different angles to produce a two-tone effect; also known as Shadow spray. Analytical Strength Solution -- A solution 04 + 0.025 percent tannin content. of

Air Speed Drying -- Very rapid air drying in which relatively high temperatures and controlled humidity are used. Albumins -- A kind of simple corpuscular proteins

containing sulphur and coagulable by heat and soluble in water itself (for example, egg albumin known as egg white). Alcohol Precipitation Value -- This value gives a measure of the total soluble matter in a tannin solution which may be precipitated by absolute alcohol. It is determined as follows: Take 10 ml of 2.5 percent tannin solution and evaporate to dryness to give the total soluble matter. Take another 10 ml of solubles in a 100 ml graduated flask and make up to the mark with absolute alcohol, shake and filter. Evaporate 50 ml of the filtrate in a small flask. The weight of the residue is subtracted from the weight of total solubles obtained earlier and the difference is expressed as percentage of the total soluble matter precipitated by alcohol. Aldehyde Leather -- White washable leather prepared usually from sheep or lambskin splits or degrains and tanned with formaldehyde or other aldehydes. Algaroba -- Dry pods of Caesalpinia brevifolium Baill., fare. Leguminosae, contain a vegetable tanning material; the tan content varying from about 45 to 50 percent. Algin -- Term referring to alginic acid and its derivatives, that is, sodium, potassium, ammonium or propylene glycol alginate, etc (see also `Irish Moss'). Alkaline Bating -- Bating with either pancreatic or microbial enzymes, which are active in the alkaline range, usually pH 8. Alligator -- A closely allied species of crocodile.

Aniline Dyed -- Leather that has been dyed with aniline dyes and has not received any colour from pigmented finish. Aniline Dyes -- Dyes synthesized from coal-tar products also known as synthetic dyes. Aniline Finish -- Basically a dye based finish with or without a trace of organic pigments. Aniline Finished --A natural or dyed leather finished by application of transparent surface coating, clear or coloured with dye. Aniline Leather -- Leather finished with transparent finishing materials so that the grain pattern may be visible. Aniline Stained -- Leather that has been stained by brushing, padding or spraying aniline dyes and has not received any coating of pigmented finish. Anionic Fatliquor -- Emulsion of fats and oils in which the colloidal droplets of oil and fats are negatively charged, for example, fat liquor made with soap solution. Annatto -- A dye of vegetable origin, orange-red in colour obtained from fruits of a shrub Bixa orellana Linn., fare. Bixaceae., a native tree of South America. Antelope -� A kind of deer. In the glove trade, the term is used to describe a fine soft leather with a velvety, 2

Alligator Grained Leather -- Imitation embossed alligator grain which is put on various types of leather such as calf, sheep or side upper as distinguished from the genuine reptilian leather. Aluminium Tanning -- Tanning with basic aluminium sulphate stabilized with a masking agent like citrate. Tanning is completed by basifying topH 4.2.

IS 1640:2007 lustrous nap made from antelope sueded on the flesh side. or gazelle skin, Army Grain -- Embossed grained leather used for military leather goods (see also `Ammunition Leather' and `Russet'). Aspergillus Niger -- One of the most common mould growths found vegetable tanning vats and on leather, usually greenish or blackish colour. Assorters -- Experts in selection and sorting of hides and skins, known in the raw hide trade asj"achandars. They are usually employed by the purchasing firms. They come to the aarhat, sort the hides and act as the buyer's judges about the price they can pay on assorter's report. Assorters also grade hides and skins in shippers' godown for export. Assortment of Hides -- Classification of hides is done on the basis otl (a) region; (b) cure, that is, dry salted (nimkis) or wet salted; (c) quality, that is slaughtered (halali), deads (murdari), rejections oirta), or double rejections; and (d) weight, namely, lights, mediums or heavies. Each of the above regional and cure classification items are again sorted according to quality, for example, slaughtered (halali), deads (murdarr), rejections (jirta) and double rejections. Astringency -- lt is the property of contracting the tissues shown by many chemicals including tannins, but in its generic sense it refers to the peculiar sensation of contraction or constriction on the tongue produced by substances containing tannins.
NOTE �-A numerical classification of the various tannins and vegetable tanning materials according to their degree of astringency is not possible, since a number of factors are involved. The astringency appears to be a function of the molecular size of the tannin, the proportion of tannin to total solub Ies (degree of purity), the hydrogen ion concentration of the solution, the electrical charge of the particles, nature of anions and neutral salts present (acid-salt ratio), temperature, and tannin content of the solution,

Antelope Finish, Suede -- Lambskin, calfskin sueded and finished to resemble

goatskin or antelope.

Anthrax -- An acute disease in animals caused by a spore forming rod-shaped organism Bacillus anthracis. Anthrax Bacillus produces anthrax. -- The micro-organism that

Anthrax Spore -- A resistant form of Bacillus anthr-acis which gives the anthrax infection. Anti-blushing Agent --A material added to a lacquer to prevent precipitation of one or more of the solid constituents of the lacquer (see also `Blushing'). Antique Grain -- A surface pattern of markings or

creases, usually irregular, in which the hollows or valleys are given a contrasting colour to produce a twotone or two-colour effect. The creases are produced by embossing, boarding or other similar means. Antique Leather -- Leather of rough, irregular and wrinkled grain produced by pleating the skins and creasing them lightly in sacks or nets and treating them in strong tan solutions. Antique leathers are dyed to multi-coloured effects. The leather is used for fimiture and automobile upholstering. Apron Leather -- Leather made from heavy sheepskins or cattle hide splits and used in making apron, or dress for the forepart of the body. Aqueous medium. Finishes -- Finishes dispersed in water

Arabian Goatskins -- Tine skins from Arabia. These are of good texture and reasonably fine grain. They are usually well flayed and ei%ciently preserved by salting. Arabian Sheep -- The Arabian sheep are of two classes, namely: (a) black faced (or black headed), and (b) white faced. The hairy covering of both types is not sotl enough to be classed as wool and is of little value. These sheep are small and not overfed so that the skin arc not greasy nor is their texture 100SCor weak. Areolar Tissue -- The fibrous and fatty tissues which connect hide or skin loosely to the underlying parts of the animal body. Areolar Tissue Sheath --A form of loose connective tissue composed of cells and delicate collagen and elastic fibres interlacing in all directions and enclosing hide tibres. Arm Staking by hand. -- A process employed to soften skin

Automobile Leather motor car cushions.

-- Leather used for upholstering

Avaram, Tarwad or Tawar -- A shrub, Cassia auriculata Buch. Ham., fare. Leguminosze, growing in Southern, Western and Central India. The dried avcwam bark delivered to Indian tanneries usually has a tannin content of about 18 percent with about 10 percent of soluble non-tans. It is the most valuable tan stuff found in India, and is extensively used in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra for the production of East India tanned leather. Ayeb -- Flaw, defect. B B -- An abbreviation denoting the best quality, for example, BDS, meaning Best Dacca Slaughtered; MBS, meaning Best Meherpur Slaughtered. 3

IS 1640:2007 Babul Bark, Kikar -- The babul or kika~ tree Acacia aruhicu Wind., fare. Leguminosaz; the bark of this tree is the most important tanning material of northern India. Large supplies are obtained from Uttar Pradesh and the Punjab while a fair amount is also obtained from Bengal. The tannin content of the bark varies; sometimes it is as high as 20 percent, but the average of the bark delivered to the tanneries is about 12 percent. The pods which contain 12 to 19 percent of tannin or 18 to 27 after the removal of seeds, arc used for making a fairly light coloured firm leather. The Sudan pods, called Santpods (tannin content of 40 percent in de-seeded pods), are used in local tanneries to produce a pinkish-white leather of good quality. Bachheras or Bachus -- Hindi names for calfskins often used in the trade. Back -- Butt with the shoulder portion. Back Boarding -- Boarding in, merely to soften it. Bacterial leather with flesh side Barometer -- A modified hydrometer measuring the density of tan liquors. OBk = (sp gr-1 ) x 1000 Bark, Quercitron -- Bark of Querctis velutinu Lam. used for Bag Trade industry. Split -- Split obtained from bag making

Banaras Hide -- A variety of cow hide obtainable from the East and South East of Uttar Pradesh. They arc not as spready as Patnas and Darbhangas. They are air-dried and are usually fairly clean-fleshed. Band Knife -- An endless band of steel sharpened cm one edge. Band Knife Splitting Machine -- Splitting machine fitted with a band knife used for splitting the hides and skins laterally into different layers. Barbed Wire Scratches -- Scratches in hides and skins caused by protruding points of barbed wire. 13areilly Hide -- Hides from Bareilly, Rampur, Moradabad and the adjoining region of Uttar Pradesh.

Flora -- Total content of bacteria.

Badly Shaped Head ---Head cut off along a line which is not perpendicular to its longitudinal axis. Badly Shaped Shanks -- Shanks cut off along a line which is not perpendicular to its longitudinal axis. Bag Hide --A leather produced usually from cowhide by vegetable tanning for making various kinds of bags, trunks, suitcases and other travel goods. The Icather is flexible and may be plain or embossed in attractive patterns, gbat grain being the most common and coloured. It is split to a suitable thickness and sometimes hand or machine boarded. Bag Tannage -- An indigenous process of tanning in which delimed hides after pre-tanning lightly in light tan liquor are sewn up in bags of which onc cnd is open. The bags are tilled with ground tanstuffs and hung from an overhead horizontal pole over a shallow earthenware vat or masonry pit. Water is poured into the bag at its open end or mouth and is allowed to percolate through the tanstuff, extracting the tannin therefrom. The tan liquor so formed 00ZCSout through the pores of the hide and drips into the vat underneath. The liquor which collects in the vat is taken in a bucket and poured in at the top of the bag over and over again. The repeated percolation of the liquor through the tanstuff makes it gradually stronger enabling the hide tibrcs to absorb more and more tannin. Continuance of the process for 6 to 8 days is sufficient for tanning even a thick buffalo hide through. It is a very quick tanning process and is extensively practiced in India on a cottage scale for making sole leather from buffalo hides. Usually babul bark is used for tanning in North India and spent myrabolan liquor in South India. 4

SYn. Q. ~iHCfOYiU Bark and Q. %Linn. `Quercitron Bark'). fare. Fagaceze, used in tanning and for dyeing. (see also `Quercitron Bark'). Bark Tannage -- The process of tanning hides and skins with vegetable tanning materials. Bark Tanned -- Leather vegetable tanned mainly by means of the tannins contained in the barks of trees, the hides and skins in process coming in contact with the raw bark. Bark Wattle, Bark Mimosa -- One of the most important tanning materials. Besides the black wattle Acacia mearnsii De Wind., syn. A. mollis-sima auct. non Wind., A. decurrens Wind. var mollis Lindl., fare. Leguminosae, there are several other Australian wattles that have been exploited or cultivated as a source of tan-bark; notable amongst these being the green wattle (Acacio decun-ens Wind.), the silver or blue wattle Acacio ealbata Link. syn. A. deczwens Wind. var. dealbata Maiden. and the golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha Benth.). The black, green and the silver wattle (as known in South Africa) are closely allied species and were at one time regarded as different varieties of the same species Acacia decwrens. The tannin content of the silver wattle is usually about 20 percent but its tanning effect is much darker than the black wattle. The green wattle possesses bark, equally rich in tannin as that of the black wattle (30 to 45 percent), but produces a much more highly coloured leather. The golden wattle bark contains a high proportion of tannin (over 40 percent) even higher than that of the black wattle, but yields a more highly coloured infusion.

IS 1640:2007 Two species of wattle, namely, Acacia dealbata Link., and Acacia decuwerzs Wind., have been introduced in the Indian sub-continent, especially in South India. Samples of South Indian Wattle have been found to contain 39 percent tannin. Wattle extract has proved particularly well suited to the rapid methods of tanning heavy leather. One of the advantages of the extract is that it does not form sludge in the tan pit to any extent. Bark, Willow -- Bark of the willow tree, Salix spp., fare. Salicaceae. Baseball Leather -- Leather used for covers of baseballs. The better grades of balls have covers of alum-tanned horsehide. Some cheaper grades are made of kip and sheepskins. Basic Dyestuffs -- See `Dyes'. Bate Pricks and skins. -- Pin holes visible on overbated hides

Bate Burns -- Skins damaged by too violent an action of bacterial bates. Bath, Chromic Acid (Chromic Acid Liquor) -- A name applied to the chromic bath used as the first bath in the two-bath chrome tanning process. Bath, Hypo (Hypo Liquor) -- Name applied to the solution of hypo used as the second or the reducing bath in the two-bath process of chrome tanning. Bath, Reducing -- Reducing liquor or hypo bath.

Basicity of Chromic Sulphate -- When pure chromic su]phatc is dissolved in water, it reacts chemically with water and produces an acid solution. More than one half of the acid thus formed can be neutralized with alkali, without causing precipitation of chromium hydroxide. The proportion of the acid that has been neutralized, to that producible from the pure chromic salt, expressed in percentage, is termed as the percent basicity of the chromic salt. Basitication -- Treating the mineral tanned stock with a mild alkali like sodium bicarbonate with a view to form large aggregate of metallic compounds: a) By putting in additional OH groups onto the metal complex so that linear polymerization of the metal complex takes place through elation, and By forming additional ionized carboxyls nccdcd for complexation with the tanning metal. basicity, Proctor basicity

Batik Effect -- Dye designs made by dyes diffusing through the cracks on a fabric coated with a sizing material (i.e. materials which can be removed later on by washing starch or wax). Cracking can be brought about in a variety of ways such as staking, dry milling, embossing, etc. Baume -- A calibration acids) that is reducible formulae: a) b) scale (for liquids, especially to sp gr by the following

Basicity -- See Schorlemmer and Freiberg basicity.

Basil -- Undyed and unfinished vegetable tanned sheep or lambskin, of comparatively large size. Bastard --A term applied to sheep having hair. There is no biological verification of the notion that sheep and goats will interbreed producing a sheep with hair. Bate -- A mixture of deliming chemical and proteolytic enzymes, used for removal of mm-essential proteins like globular proteins, mucins, elastins and residues of keratin by chemically reacting and dissolving them along with some fats from limed hides and skins. They also remove lime from hides and skins besides the others. Bates contain proteolytic and lipatic enzymes and suitable deliming chemicals. Bating renders the final leather fine and silky on the surface and soft and supple to the feel. 5

Beam -- A convex, wooden slab covered on top with zinc sheet, placed at a downward slope to the floor, Alternatively, the split or hollowed trunk of a palm tree may be used. Raw stock is placed on the beam for trimming, fleshing, unhairing or scudding by hand. Beam House -- Department of tannery in which raw stock is washed, soaked, limed, unhaired, bated and prepared for tanning. Beam House Operations -- Soaking, liming, unhairing, fleshing, deliming, scudding, bating and pickling. Beaver Lamb -- Sheep or lamb skin with short fine wool, which has been dressed with the wool on, dyed and finished by a process giving a weather-resistant straightness and brightness to the wool lustered by ironing with formaldehyde on a rotary iron.

IS 1640:2007 Bellows Hide -- Curried, flexible and air-proof leather made from split hide, used for making bellows. Belly --Part of hide from under side of animal, usually less valuable than other portions. In flaying, hides arc slit along the centre line of the belly so that when the hide is taken off, the belly is divided into two halves one lying on each side of the hide. Belting Butts �- Butts tanned and finished for making machine belting. Belting that has produce suitable Butt -- The butt portion of selected cattle hide been specially tanned, curried and dressed to strong, flexible leather with minimum stretch, for the manufacture of transmission belting. Bleaching (1) ---- The process of removing oxidized tannins and insoluble materials from the surface layers of leather, in order to prevent cracking of the grain and to lighten the colour. It is performed by dipping the leather in a weak acidic solution to render the tannin readily soluble, dipping again in water, neutralizing in weak acid solution and washing. Bleaching (2) -- The process of lightening the colour of chrome leather by suitable chemical treatment or precipitating white pigment in the surface of the leather. Bleaching Extract -- Extract used for making the co!our of dark tanned leather light and pale. Bleaching Syntan -� Auxiliary syntan which when complexed to chrome in a chrome leather makes its blue colour lighter. Bleeding -- The transfer of materials exuded from leather to other material that comes into contact with it. It is usually designated as staining, Blended
myrobalan

Belting Lace -- Chrome tanned back, about 2.5 mm thick, heavily dressed with natural grease, suitable for cutting into strips for the purpose of joining transmission belting.
NOTE -- The oil-treated back is generally known as `Helvctia leather'.

Belting Leather -- Leather for machine belting generally made from the butt portion of high grade cattle hides. Belt Leather -- Leather used for waist belts. It is usually considered a subclass of fancy leather and usually made from cattle hides, sheep and goatskins. Bend -- Half of a hide with the shoulders and belly portions trimmed off. It is the best portion of the hide. Bends of thick hides are used for making SOICS of boots and shoes, machine belting, etc. Bengal Blacks -- See `Lizard Skins' Beparis -- Dealers in hides and skins who collect hides and skins in the villages or from slaughter houses and sell them in larger centres. Binder -- A filmogen or film forming polymeric material used to bind pigment particles tenaciously to the surface of the leather. Birch Oil -- See `Oil, Birch.' Bisulphiting -- The treatment given to hot solutions of vegetable tan extracts with sodium bisulphitc in order to increase their solubilities. Black Catechu -- According to Pharmacopoeia of India, 1966, black catechu is synonymous with KA TTHA. It consists of the dried aqueous extracts prepared from the heartwood of Acacia catechu Wind and Acacia chundra Wind. Blackwood -- A native of Australia Acacia melanoxylon R. Br. introduced in India, common in the Nilgiris; the bark contains approximately 13 percent tannins. 6

or mangroves,

or myrobalan

and cutch, etc, used to attain optimum yield and desired quality in leather ( see Tanning Extract). Blisters -- Damages on skins usually caused by putrefaction as a result of bad or insufficient curing, preservation or sun-drying. Block Printing -- Printing using separate wooden blocks having curved designs for each colour. The total appearance will be the cumulative effect of all the colours applied. Bloom �- A light-coloured deposit of ellagic acid appearing on the grain surface of leather tanned with certain pyrogallol tannins, such as myrobalans, valonia, and divi-divi. The appearance may be objectionable for some purposes, but bloom does not significantly affect the other physical properties of the leather. Blue -- Usually in the phrase `in the blue'. Applied to hides or skins that have been chrome-tanned but not dyed nor fatliquored. Blushing -- A milky opalescence which sometimes develops on leather as a film of lacquer dries and is due to the deposition of moisture from the air or precipitation, of one or more of the solid constituents of the lacquer or due to both these conditions. Boarded Leather -- Leather grained or creased up by working with a cork faced board. This working is called boarding or graining because it produces different patterns on the grain side of the leather. It also softens the leather considerably. Boarding is also done by boarding machine consisting of cork or rubber covered rollers.

IS 1640:2007 Boarding -- To strike a grain pattern on the leather. This was done formerly by working the leather in a suitable manner with a cork faced wooden board from which the operation has derived the name. It can also be achieved by machines. The operation is also known as graining (see `Gaining'). Boardy --Adjective applied to stiff, inflexible leather. lost and the value of the entire hide is considerably reduced. Bran Drench -- A fermented infusion of wheat bran extensively used in tanneries for deliming. Branding -- The treatment of pelt with bran infusion. Branning opens up the pores of the skin besides dissolving the lime in the pelt. Brazil Wax --Also called camauba wax. It is obtained as an exudation from the leaves of the wax palm Coperniia cerzfera Mart., fare. Palmae. It is one of the hardest and most expensive of the commercial waxes. Brazil Wood -- Peach wood or pemambuco wood obtained from Caesal-pinia echinatu Lam., fare. Leguminosae and several Brazilian spp. which yield a red colouring matter called brasilin. With alum mordant, it produces a red shade and with chrome mordant a violet shade. It is used to some extent in Ieathcr dyeing. Breaking Iron -- Blunt iron knife used for breaking hides on the beam. Breaking on Beam -- Dry hides and skins are often laid upon the beam after soaking and worked on the flesh side with a blunt unhairing knife which scrapes off bits of the adhering flesh and softens the hides and skins by its stretching action. Break of Leather -- The tiny wrinkles formed on the grain surface of leather when it is bent, grain inward in a fine break. There are many fine wrinkles per linear unit in contrast to a coarse break. Bridle Leather -- Strong, flexible type of harness leather of reasonably uniform thickness with a plain finish and a close shaved flesh. Made from ox or cow hide, vegetable tanned and curried. Brined, Dry -- Hides or skins treated with brine and dried or dry salted. Brined, Wet -- Hides and skins treated with brine and kept wet or wet salted. Brisket -- The part of the hide covering the breast.

Boil Test -- Testing a piece of fully hydrated leather to check whether there is any shrinkage after placing in boiling water for 2-3 minutes only. When the leather retains the original area, chrome tanning is considered completed. Bookbinding Leather -- Leather generally made from calf, sheep and goatskins and used for bookbinding. Bot Fly, Warble Fly -- Of the family Oestridae, many species of which produce holes in the backbone region of the hide. Bottom Hide -- Hide used for making shoe bottoms. Bottoming -- Coating the surface of leather with a solution of mucilage or like material, for closing the pores of the leather. This serves as the foundation for finishes. Bottom Leather -- Leather used for shoe bottoms.

Bound Organic Substance -- The difference between 100 and the sum of the values of the percentage of volatile matter, water insoluble ash, solvent extractable substances, hide substances and water soluble substances in a leather. It is expressed as percent by weight of a leather. Box Calf -- Formerly, a full-chrome flexible black calf leather with a fine box grain produced by boarding the leather in two directions. An identical leather in brown is called willow calf but these distinctions arc losing much of this significance as box calf is now made in a wide range of colours. Principally used for footwear but also for hand bags, golf bags, etc. Box Finish -- The finish in which the leather is glazed and boarded two-way, once from neck to butt and then from belly to belly. Box Grain -- The two-way boarding of box finish which produces fair, square shaped creases on the grain surface of the leather. Box Sides -- Leather manufactured from cattle hides by the chrome process and finished with box grain. The hide is slit into two halves along the spine, each of which is called a side. Branded Hides -- Hides with marks of scars caused by drawing various figures on the body of cattle with a red hot iron. The portion of the hide thus branded is 7

Bronze Leather -- A variety of leather which is purposely finished with a bronze appearance. Bronze leathers are made by staining with concentrated solution of basic aniline dyes or by coating the leather with bronze powder or leaf. Bronzing (1) -- Excessive concentration of crystallized dyestuff on the surface of the leather tending to give a metallic sheen. Bronzing is a dichroic effect produced by light reflected from the surface of the dyed leather. This happens when a spot has a different refractive index from the environment.

IS 1640:2007 Bronzing effect is obtained brown on exposure to sun. when Icather becomes Buffed Leather -- Leather from which the top surface of the flesh side has been removed by an abrasive or bladed cylinder or, less generally, by hand. In the case of upholstery leather the buffing process is invariably carried out by machine though it is sometimes incorrectly described as `hand buffed'. See Corrected grain, Machine buff. Buffing ��A very light cut of grain portion taken from the surface of cattle hide. An operation to produce a fine nap on leather by the action of an emery wheel (see also `Fluffing' and `Snuffing'). Buffing (1) -- The thin grain layer of leather removed from a cattle hide by the splitting machine. In Spain the buffing may be from any hide or skin. Buffing (2) -- The process of more or less removing the flesh layer by abrasion. See also Buffed leather. Buffing (3) -- Removal of the flesh side of the leather by mechanical abrasion to produce a suede effect or to reduce the substance. Synonymous with flu fflng and now in more common use. In Spain the buffhg may be from any hide or skin. In North America the thin grain layer of leather removed from cattle hide by the splitting machine. Buffing Slicker -- Hand slicker used for removing the coarse fibres of the flesh side of leather in the manufacture of russet and waxed leather. Buff Leather -- An oil leather, flexible and dry, manufactured after the grain side has been scoured off. The leather is made from buffalo hides as well as from heavy ox and cow hides, usually by tanning with fatty substances. It possesses a cream or white surface and is finished on the grain side with a velvet like nap. It is used for polishing of metals. Buffs -- Abbreviated form for buffaloes. for sole leather made

Bronzing (2) -- Making leather brown by exposure to the sun or making it shine with a metallic lustre. Bruising outwards. -- Softening leather by flexing grain

Brush Coat -- The second coat of varnish applied in finishing patent leather. Brush Colouring -- The application of dyestuff to leather with a brush or swab, the leather being laid on a table. Also called table dyeing. Brush-Off Effect -- Brushed appearance. The brush marks are made as follows: Over the pigmented resin coat having excellent adhesion and flexibility with complete coverage, a high gloss, clear lacquer coat is applied and plated. A third lacquer coat with a contrasting colour is applied. The film formed now should be tough enough to provide the usual resistance properties, yet soft enough to be removed by the brushing action. The clear lacquer underneath is a guarantee that the brushing action does not go through the base coat. Now, a rotating brush is applied to the tinish surface and the surface finish layer is removed to make a contrast with the base coat colour. The degree of contrast is controlled during brushing. Brushing Machine -- A machine to sweep or clean with a brush; a scouring machine. Buck -- Actually, leather from the skins of a male deer. It is the same as buckskin but nowadays, the tarn is applied to suede shoe upper leather, dressed and finished in the same way as real buckskin though not made from deerskin. Buck Side -- Cattle hide shoe upper leather with grain surface buffed to simulate genuine buckskin. Buckskin -- Soft leather made of deerskins or Bulkskins used for shoes and gloves and to some extent in clothing. Leather finished from the split or under cut of deerskin must be described as `split skin'. Only the outer cut of the skin from which the surface grain has been removed may be correctly defined as genuine buckskin. Buffalo Hides or Buff-Hides -- The skins of a buffalo, Bos bubalus. Buffaloes are principally found in the states of Assam, Bihar, Tamil Nadu, Orissa, Punj ab and Uttar Pradesh. Buffalo Liming -- A method of liming which was practised in America in which hides were first treated with a solution of calcium chloride followed by a solution of caustic soda. Buff Calf -- Leather made from the skin of a young or immature buffalo. 8

Buff-Sole -- An abbreviation from buffalo hide.

Buffer Index -- The number in ml of 1 N hydrochloric acid or 1 N sodium hydroxide solution required to be added to 100 ml of tannin infusion or liquor at 20"BK in order to alter its pH by 1 unit. For accuracy, the buffer index should be determined on a portion of the titration curve corresponding to at least 2 pH units and lying between pH 2.5 and 5.0. Burnishable Leathers -- Leathers, which develop a polish on being rubbed just as in the case of boot polishing. The special effect is achieved by the inclusion of a wax treatment in the effect coat formation. Burnishing -- Polishing by machine to give the shoe upper a bright, glossy finish. On better grade shoes. the sole and heel edges are washed and burnished.

Bursting Strength -- Strength of leather to resist bursting or cracking of the grain under strain. Butcher Cuts -- Cuts or gashes in hides and skins caused by butchers while flaying. Butt -- A roughly rectangular part of a hide representing the part covering the back and upper regions of animal and remaining after the shoulder and belly portions are cut off. The butt is the best portion of the hide being the thickest and most compact in structure. When cut along the centre, the butt divides into two halves each of which is called a bend. Butt Split -- The flesh layer obtained by splitting the butt by a splitting machine. Butt Striking -- A rapid succession of blows from a blunt edge upon the grain surface of the butt. The working tool is usually a steel blade or it may be a slate like stone. The object is to remove bloom and reds from the grain of the leather. Batty -- Hide or leather with thick butt. c C -- An abbreviation used by the hide shippers to denote: (a) cow hides, (b) the classification Commissariats, and (c) cured. CCS mean Cow Commissariats Slaughtered. Cabretta -- Skins of hair sheep or bastards. These have no wool, but straight hairlike a goat. They produce a tough and tine leather suitable for gloves, shoes and roller skins for mills. Calcium Soap -- Soap produced by the combination of fatty acids and lime. In the liming of hides and skins, lime acts on the natural grease of hides and skins and gives a calcium soap which is mostly removed from hides and skins by the process called scudding. Capeskin or Cape Leather -- Term commonly applied to all glove and garment leather made from sheepskins with the natural grain retained. This should be correctly confined to leather from South African hair sheep. Genuine capeskin from South Africa is a light, flexible, fine grained durable leather generally superior to the wool sheepskins of the same or other places. When used to designate capeskins other than the South African, it should be qualified as `Domestic Capeskin', `Spanish Capeskin', etc. It should never be applied to a skiver. Captive Bolt -- A pistol used as an alternative to the pole axe or knife for stunning, while slaughtering cattle. When fired, a plunger or bolt in the barrel penetrates the brain. Cohesion -- The amount of water which collagen or gelatin takes up under any given conditions is controlled by the balance between two opposing forces, one the force of osmotic pressure which causes water to pass into the protein and the other the resistance of the protein to the distension caused by the entry of water, conveniently termed as the cohesive force of the protein. In the cold sweat process, the temperature is not raised. Collagen -- Protein contained in connective tissue, cartilage and bones, the chief protein of raw hides and skins. Cordovan, Cordvan, Cordvane, Cordwain -- Spanish leather or crup leather. An article of medieval times, produced in Cordova, after the Moorish conquest of Spain. Damping -- After the leather has been dried in order to set the fiber, it must again be damped back or sammcd before the finishing processes can be carried out. Two methods are employed. The first consists of dipping the stock in warm water for a short time and then laying them in a pile overnight covered with a tarpaulin; and the second in placing the leather in a pile with damp saw dust between each hide or skin and then covering the pile completely with more damp saw dust. By either of these methods, the stock becomes uniformly damp, without containing an excess of moisture in any part. Darbhangas -- The best kind of cow hides from Western Bihar. They are air-dried, usually not so spready as the Pumeas but of equally good texture, well shaped, clean as regards flesh and grain, and sometimes procurable in the framed condition. -- Cleansing wool of fur skins.

Degras, Moellen -- Uncombined fish oil pressed out of sheepskin splits in the manufacture of chamois leather. As oiled skins are exposed to air oxidation in this process, the uncombined oil pressed out is also oxidized and thereby gets the valuable property of easy emulsification. On account of this property, degras is much used in leather manufacture for fat-liquoring and currying, so much so that it is now also artificially manufactured by oxidizing cod or fish oil by blowing steam and air into it. The type of cod oil used in chamoising in the continent of Europe remains more or less liquid in the oil tanned chamois leather and, therefore, can be easily pressed out. This when compounded forms the moellen degras of commerce. Degrain -- Suede leather, finished on the flesh side, the grain having been wholly or partially removed after tanning by splitting or abrasion. Decreasing -- Removing grease in the case of pickled sheepskins by drumming the stock with kerosene, water and salt; in the case of leather, by extracting the dried leather with any suitable solvent. Degree of Tannage -- Number per 100 parts of hide substance. of parts of fixed tan.

Dermatitis -- A disease of the derma or true skin occasionally accompanied by intense irritation. It can be caused by contact with chrome liquors, formaldehyde or mineral oils. Dermis (Derma) -- The true skin or that part from which leather is produced. Also called `Corium'. I)ewlaps -- The loose hanging skin under the throat of cattle, where the butcher (flayer) first inserts his knife when slaughtering or flaying. Dhawa, Dhaura -- Tanning material obtained from the twigs and leaves of the tree, Anogeissus latd'olia Wall. fare. Combretaceae. Average tannin content of the leaves is about 32 percent while a mixture consisting of young leaves and twigs mostly broken called dhawa (sumac) has a tan content of 38.5 percent. The leaves have good bleaching action almost approaching that of Italian sumac. Difference Figure -- The difference between the pH value of a solution and its tenfold dilution. It is a measure for the strength of acids and bases. This value can never exceed the value 1. Diplococci -- Pairs of spherical bacteria.

Doubles --Also called double rejections or wrappers. These are very inferior hides which cannot even be selected as `Rejections'. They are often rotten in places, have marks due to the pecking and scratching of vultures, badly branded or badly cut. Drape -- The property by which a dressing material covers parts of body following its contours (that is, ups and downs). Drawn Flanks -- Flanks of skins and leathers that have shrunk and show furrowed lines on the grain surface over the underlying blood vessels. Drawn Grain -- Shrivelled grain like the skin of a dried apple. Drawn grain arises when the grain surface gets tanned and fixed in area while the substance of the hide is in a more extended condition. Drenching -- The process of deliming with fermented wheat bran. Drench Pit -- A pit in which wheat bran is allowed to ferment and in which the hides are subsequently handled for deliming. Dressed Hides -- Tanned hides, curried or otherwise finished, for various purposes, such as belting, harness and saddlery, travel goods and for upholstery. Dressing Agents -- Oils, fats, waxes, etc, used for dressing and finishing hides and skins. Dressing Leather -- Vegetable tanned unsplit hides which may be dressed to suit the purpose for which they are to be used, such as for harness, saddlery and other mechanical purposes. 16

Dipped Dressed --A term used in currying to describe leather which has been impregnated by immersion in hot grease. Direct Dyestuff -- See `Dyes.'

Discoloration or Red Spots --As a rule, these spots are superficial since it is mainly the salt which is discolored and not the skin itself. They disappear almost completely after the first beamhouse operation, namely, soaking. Divi-Divi -- Tanning material cbtained from the dried pods of the tree Cuesalpinia coriaria (Jacq.) Wind. fare. Leguminosae. The tan content of the pods varies from 28 to 41 percent. It is usually employed in combination with other tanstuffs chiefly as a substitute for gambir (from Uncaria g-ambir Roxb. fare. Rubiaceae ) and valonia, from Quercu.s macrolepsis kotschy fare. Fagaceae in the tanning industry. The leather produced is of light yellowish tint. The worlds' supply of divi-divi comes chiefly

IS 1640:2007 Dried Hides -- The method of curing hides by airdrying is practiced usually in the North, North-West and other drier parts of India. It is not very common in the humid climates of Bengal and Assam. Most of the Indian hides are cured by air-drying in which the weight of the green hide is reduced to about a third by drying. Exposure to hot mid-day sun' is avoided as it causes case-hardening and consequently sunburns or blisters. In India, the best months for air-drying are those of winter when the air is dry and the sun not too hot. Airdried hides are known as `flints' because of their hardness. Before export they are dipped in a solution of preservative for protection against insects (see also `Air-Dried Hides'). Drum-Head Leather -- Parchment or raw hide from sheepskins or calfskins for musical drums. Drums -- Cylindrical vessels made of wood, mounted on suitable axles so that they are capable of revolving freely. They are usually equipped inside with pegs or shelves for lifting the stock. Goods may be entered through a door which can be closed watertight. These are used for keeping the hides and skins in good movement during various stages of tanning. Drum Stuffing -- Incorporating grease and fats into the leather by using a specially fitted drum. Dry Dip -- A strong solution of vegetable tan extracts in which dry sole leather is dipped preparatory to second bleaching and second oil wheeling to increase the firmness and solidity of the finished leather and to add weight. Drying Loft -- Space in a tannery where dried leather is kept for crushing; or stored awaiting selection for subsequent treatment. Dry Milling -- Tumbling pressed leather in a revolving drum to open it up and remove the creases, Dry Pickling -- A method of curing skins from wool sheep with sodium sulphate and sodium chloride. Sometimes hypo also is used with a little acid. Sulphuric acid is used in modem processes. Dry-Salted Hides and Skins -- Hides and skins cured by the process of dry-salting. The salt used for curing is khari salt which is a natural product consisting mainly of sodium sulphate mixed with earthy matters. A few coats of a soupy solution of this salt are applied on the flesh side of hides and skins, and then dried in the sun. This method is followed mainly in the NorthEast part of India where the climate is damp. Dry Tunnel -- A tunnel in which damp leather is placed for drying in a current of air, often under conditions of controlled temperature and relative humidity. 17 Dubbin �- Mixture of cod or fish oil and tallow in suitable proportions used for currying leather. More cod oil is used in the mixtures in winter and slightly more tallow in summer. Dull Finish -- See `Finish, Dull'. Dusters -- In the older process of sole leather tanning, a small amount of ground tanning material, 1 to 1.5 kg per butt, was sprinkled between the butts. The two strongest handlers were called `dusters' and formed a link between the handlers proper and the layers (see also `Handler'). Dusting -- Spreading ground raw vegetable tanning materials over and between the hides entering the layer vats, adding to the tannin strength of liquors. This was a common method before concentrated tanning extracts came into use. Dye -- A dye (or dyestuff) is most commonly an organic compound which may be used to impart colour to a substance. It may be used for the colouring of animal, vegetable or synthetic fibres and similar products [such as wool, silk, leather or fur, cotton, linen, paper, rayon, nylon, or other materials (such as oils, waxes, rubber or plastics, etc)]. Dyes may be soluble in water or may be made so by a simple chemical reaction. Insoluble colouring matters are called `pigments'. Dyes may be classified in accordance with their (Nitro-, azo-, constitution chemical Triphenylmethanes, etc), or their method of application. The class of dyestuffs leather industry are: a) more commonly used in the

Divect Dyestuffs -- Dyestuffs which dye cotton fibre directly, without the aid of mordants. Method of application to leather is similar to that of acid colours, but no addition of acid is required in the dye-bath. Direct dyestuffs, or substantive colours have got good aff]nity for chrome tanned leather and are used for dyeing chrome leather, specially blacks. Basic Dyestufls -- These are aniline dyes which are compounds of an organic base with an inorganic acid usually hydrochloric. They have great affinity for tannins and, therefore, dye vegetable tanned leather directly. They have little affinity for chrome leather which has to be mordanted with tannin if basic dyes are to be employed. Developed Dyestuff -- Dyestuffs whose colours are developed by chemical treatment after application to the leather. This is

East India Kips (E. I. Kips) -- Crust tanned kips (cow hide) from India are called kips, because they arc not big enough to be classed with cattle hides of other countries and not so small as to be regarded as calfskins. Hides below 11 kg as green weight or 5 kg dry weight arc regarded as kips. The term is applied to raw and dressed or vegetable tanned Indian hides, more particularly to the latter. Indian kips partly tanned with vegetable tan material (awwam bark and wattle bark) are mainly exported to England where they are usually dressed for russet lining, box side leather, bag leather and a variety of other purposes. Egg Yolk -- Yellow of the egg. It forms a constituent of alum tawing paste. Egg yoke is very useful particularly in the treatment of gloving and clothing leathers of all tannages. Elangaram -- Indigenous method of deliming carried out by water, assisted by trampling of the hides. Elastic material it, such bellows, Gusset -- A triangular flexible piece of inserted in a garment to enlarge or strengthen as the side pieces for extension in purses, etc. Ellagic Acid -- It is a yellowish powder, odourless, tasteless, insoluble in water even at 10O�C but slightly soluble in alcohol, having the chemical formulae C1406H8, and used in medicine. Present in galls. Ellagitannin --A class of hydrolyzable tannins related to the gallotannins (from plant galls). They produce bloom on leather and occur in myrobalans, valonia, divi-divi and a number of other well known tanning materials. Ellu -- Dried bark of the elm tree Ulmus rubya Muhl. syn. U. fu/va Michx. fare. Ulmaceae, containing gums and tannin. Elongation -- The extension between bench marks produced by a tension force applied to a test piece. It is expressed by a percentage of the original distance between the marks on the unstretched test piece. Elongation at Break -- The extension between bench marks produced by a tension force applied to a test piece at the time of its rupture. It is calculated by taking the difference between the original length and the length at the time of rupture under the tension force, expressed as a percentage of the original length. Elongation at Specified Load -- The extension between bench marks produced by a specified tension force applied to a test piece. It is calculated by taking the difference between the original length and the length at the specified load, expressed as a percentage of the original length. Euphorbiaceae. found wild or cultivated, throughout greater part of India, used in medicine and is a rich source of vitamin C and pectin. The fruits, bark and leaves of the tree are rich in tannins, the tannin content being approximately 28 percent, 8 to 21 percent and 22 percent, respectively. The tannin is of condensed type. Elk Leather -- Chrome retanned cow hide leather treated with grease for softening and waterproofing. A purely trade term in America for cattle hide shoe leather of a special tannage and finish. Enamelled Leather -- Originally, the term signified a leather similar to patent or japanned leather but with an embossed grain. It was made for gladstone bags, brief bags and document cases. Its chief use today is for head leather (hoods) of motor cars. Enameling -- The name applied to the process of repeatedly coating the grain side of leather with boiled linseed oil or cellulose varnish with intermediate drying by which shining upholstery leather is made. The process is similar to japanning with this difference that the latter name is restricted to coating the flesh side of the hides with the varnish. Enamellng is followed by graining or embossing, while `japanning', which gives patent leather, is kept plain. Enzyme Bates -- Artificial bates which owe their activity to enzyme. Mostly, the enzymes present in the pancreatic juice, namely, trypsin and steapsin, are so utilized. They dissolve and remove some constituents of the hide. Enzymes -- Biocatalyst of biological origin and are characterized by their extraordinary specificity and reactivity in living systems. Erector-Pilimuscle -- One of the tiny involuntary muscles of the skins associated with hair that causes goose pimples to form, the hair to stand on end and oil to flow from sebaceous glands to the skin surface, a muscle active in the thermostat mechanism of the skin. Ethyl Acetate Value -- Number of milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to saponify the esters (ethyl acetate) in one gram of the sample. Eucalyptus -- Name of genus of plants. Kino-impregnated bark is available from many species of eucalyptus which are felled for timber. The tannin content of kino is high (fee also `Kino'). IS 1640:2007 Falling -- To deplete or remove the swelling of limed pelts by bating. Falling Solution -- Saturated solution of sodium chloride used in pickling hides and skins for export in the pickled condition. It is called falling solution because the stock previously treated in pickling with a solution of salt and sulphuric acid falls or loses its swelling when treated with saturated brine. This process of removing the swelling of the pelts is known as `Depletion'. Fancy Leather -- Light leathers of different shades of colour and finish for making artistic and fancy leather goods. Finished Leather -- Tanned leather processed and finished to the extent that can be used directly without any further treatment for fabrication into industrial and consumer items or parts of such items. Fixed Tannin -- Tannin which is chemically fixed by protein. It is represented by the difference between 100 pcrccnt and the sum of the percentages of moisture, oils and t"ats, water soluble matter, hide substance and insoluble ash. Fixing Agent -- Chemical or mechanical agent that holds the mordants, dyes, pigments, or free vegetable tannins on the leather fibres. Flaccid -- The soft, fallen, flabby condition produced in pelts by the bating process; a depleted condition with entire absence of plumpness or rubberiness. Flank hip. -- Side of an animal between the ribs and the

Flesh Side -- Reverse side of the hide as opposed to the liairy or grain side. Flesh Split -- Hides split into two or more layers by the splitting machine. The lower layer or the layer on the flesh side is called `flesh split'. Flesh splits are tanned and finished into leather. The layer containing the grain is called `grain split' or `skiver'. The grain splits are usually more valuable for leather making than the flesh splits. Fleshy Hides -- Defective hides in which a lot of flesh has been left with a view to increasing weight. Flexural Endurance -- The number of flexes the leather withstands without any visible damage to the finish or the grain. Flints -- Air-dried Hides'. hides. Also called `Flint Dried

Flank Skins -- Skins running thin along the belly and producing a flat open grain in the leather. Flanky Finish -- Appearance of crazing, checking or flaking with or without separation of finished film. Flaying Machine -- Mechanical hand unit, replacing the flaying knife and consisting of two saw-edged circular blades placed together, moving in opposite directions and powered by electricity or compressed air. The machine is capable of producing perfectly flayed hides, but is not used for flaying skins. Fleece -- Woolly covering of a sheep or similar animal.

French Kid or French Kid Finish -- Leather tanned from kidskin by an alum process which, in the glove trade, is known as `Glove Kid'. French Morocco -- Misleading name for leather similar in appearance to Morocco but made from sheepskins. Use of this term should be discouraged Fresh Hides -- Hides taken straight from the animal carcass before curing and dressing. Frigorifico Hides -- Hides from South American meat canning plants, usually cured by the frigorifico method in which curing is done by brining the hides and subsequently strewing solid common salt on them. Frizing -- Removing the grain by hand, using a frizing knife, after liming for 30 to 40 days. The process is used for making Mocha `Glove Leather'. Fronts -- Portion of horse hides or pigskins from neck up to the end of the butt. Full-Chrome (Tanned) -- The adjective `full' is sometimes added to chrome tanned to emphasize that the leather is neither semi-chrome nor combination chrome but pure chrome. Full-Chrome Washers -- See `Chrome Washers'.

Foam Finishing -- Applying finishes onto leather in the form of a foam. High viscosity foam made of a polyurethane dispersion, pigment, filler and a foam stabilizer, when made in a mixer, is stable upto a few hours and can be remixed after longer periods. To suit the high viscosity requirements of Reversible Roller Coatcrs, foam finishes were actually developed. But, the added advantage that resulted is that more finish can be applied more economically. Though suited for full grain leathers also, it is more beneficial to damaged and hence deeply buffed leathers and splits. Fog Resistance -- Non-emission of volatile matter by leather upholstery, which can condense over the window screen in cold climate. Follicle -- Hair follicle. A small cavity or pocket in which the hair grows. Follicular Mange -- Infestation of the skin of mammals by Demodexfolliculorum which parasitizes the hair follicles or sebaceous glands of men and domestic animals. Football Leather -- Used for football covering, originally made from pigskins but is now generally made from cattle hides. Forel -- A grade of parchment made from fleshed sheepskin and having special properties of colour and surface rendering it suitable for bookbinding and fancy purposes. Formaldehyde Precipitation Value -- It is the percentage of soluble matter obtained when 10 ml of 40 percent formaldehyde solution and 5 ml of concentrated hydrochloric acid are added to 50 ml of a 0.4 + 0.025 percent tannin solution and refluxed for 30 minutes. Formaldehyde Tanning -- Process of tanning hides and skins with a solution of formaldehyde for the production of white leather. Formas Fourths Foxskins Framed -- See `Firmas'. -- Another name for low grade raw hide. -- Skins of foxes valued for their fur. -- See `Firmas'.

Full Grain -- Leather bearing the original grain surface as exposed by removal of the epidermis and with none of the surface removed by buffing, snuffhg or splitting. Full Grain (Full Top Grain) -- Term applied to the outer surface or grain portion of a hide from which only the hair has been removed. Fullness -- Characteristic plumpness of substance. Fungi -- See `Mold'. Fur -- Skins of some wild animals, covered with short fine hair, which is tanned or dressed for garments. Fur Dressing -- Dressing the fur skins. Involves besides all-important leather making operations, some modifications in the usual operations in view of the necessity of retaining the furs and some additional operations and processes to dress the furs. The modifications in the usual operations are: Green fleshing and wheel buffing on the flesh-side. Fur-on Nappalan -- Fur-on leathers where the flesh side is finished as nappalans. Galuchet -- A kind of sharkskin tanned without removal of the hard, pebbly surface. Similar to boroso leather but with a coarser grain. Ganjams -- Variety of cow hides generally of poor quality and selection obtainable from the area north of Tamil Nadu state and Ganjam in Orissa. Gash -- A cut produced on the skin by the knife or the flaying appliance, cutting into the dermis or skin substance without there being an actual perforation. Gasket Leather -- See `Hydraulic Leather'.

From this value, tannin content of a vegetable tan liquor may be obtained by multiplying this value with a factor specific to each tanning material. Gall Nuts, Galls, Oak Galls -- They are the best known of the vegetable galls (abnormal accumulations of plant tissue caused through external parasitic influence) used for tanning, especially those which have been known in the trade as Mecca, Aleppo or Turkish galls. Gouge -- Thinning of the skin caused by the knife or by the flaying appliance, without there being any actual perforation. Gouges -- A chisel with a hollow blade for cutting grooves or holes. Grain -- The surface of the unhaircd pelt or leather. The design on the outer surface of the finished leather produced by the arrangement of hair follicles, is distinct for each species of animals and each pattern is a composite of the openings of hair pores, nerve papillae and the cumulative effect of the structures underlying the surface. The grain pattern provides an easy means of identifying different type of leather. Grain Box -- Square grain, grain characteristics produced when calf and side leathers are boarded from neck to neck and from belly to belly. Grain, Brittle -- Grain which is prone to crack.

Grain Burst -- Tearing of the hair-side of the skin during flaying, whatever the process of flaying used. Grain, Corrected -- Where the grain of a leather is poor or damaged, very often it is buffed off and a finish applied which tills the buffed grain surface and hides the fact that the grain has been previously coarse or damaged. Resin finishes incorporated with highly concentrated pigment pastes and a little wax emulsion are very suitable for correcting grain finish. Grain Crack Resistance -- The load in kg/mm thickness of a leather at which cracks appear on the grain surface of the leather. Grain Damage -- Any damage to the grain side of the skin, whatever its origin or nature, causing depreciation of the skin.
NOTE --- This depreciation can bc caused in a variety of ways. Holes or abcesses, various diseases (mange, warts, etc), the aftermath of blisters, skin troubles, horn rake, rubbed hindquuters or rubbed neck, goad pricks, branding iron burse, corrosive paints, tar, various scratches (brambles, barbed wire, ckamagecaused during transportation or dragging, curry-comb marks, rope marks), scarring or gashes as a result of surgery, dog bites, etc.

Gold Kld -- Kid or fine goat leather finished with a coating of gold or gold alloy leaf. Goran, Bara Goran -- Ceriops dccandra (Griff) Dinghov syn. Ceriops roxburghiona Am., farn. Rhizophoraceae, is a shrub or a small tree found in the tidal forests of Sunderbans, east coast of India, Tenasserim, Andamans, Srilanka and various parts of Malaysia. The bark (tannin content, 20 to 37 percent) and the leaves (tannin content, 9 to 15 percent) arc important tanstuffs. The bark imparts a red colour to the leather which can be avoided to a large extent by blending it with myrobalans (Terrninalia chebula Retz. fruits) and the bark of babul (Acacia arabica Linn.) in suitable proportions, or by decolonizing and bleaching (see m'so `Mangrove'). Grain Layer -- The top layer of the corium including the hair follicles. The individual fibres of this layer arc finer than that in the rest of the corium. Grain Leather -- Any leather on which the original natural grain has been changed or altered to any degree by any process or manipulation. Grainier -- Type of surface crystallizer in which the sodium chloride crystals are raked to one end by a reciprocating mechanism, allowed to drain on an inclined table and get discharged. Grainy Leather -- Leather with too coarse or russet grain. Also leather showing marbled grain. Grassers -� Calf or kipskins taken from animals that are poorly fed and possess coarser grain. Grater -- An instrument to pulverize by rubbing.

Grain Memel (Grain, Natural) -- Grain characteristics produced when calf and suede leathers are boarded diagonally. Grain, Old -- Defect of the grain perceptible as raised and depressed patches on the grain surface. This is caused by the age of the animal and found more on bull than on cowhides. It is not possible to get a smooth leather from a hide having this defect. Grain Pattern -- See `Grain'.

Ground Drying -- Sun-drying of hides end skins for which they are spread on the ground, flesh side uppermost, and either weighed down with stones or pegged to the ground through holes around the edges. This method of drying is unsatisfactory and should be discouraged. Ground Hair --Young hair which is growing and is, therefore, still small and thin, also called short hair. This does not become loose in liming as quickly as old long hair does because its root is more firmly embedded in the skin and it is not easily removed by the action of the depilants. Growth Marks -- Marks of the fold lines on hides and skins made permanent by the hardening of the tissues in the course of ageing while being part of the live animal. Ground Fibre, Coarse or Fine -- While grinding solid

IS 1640:2007 crude tanning material for the preparation of samples for analysis, not all the material become uniformly fine. Substance' Hair Papillae --Aprojection from the dermis into the hair bulb through which nourishment is supplied to the growing hair. Hair Pulp -- The pulp to which hair is reduced by strong solutions of sodium sulphide or alkali. Hair-Pulping Methods of Unhairing -- Methods, which facilitate unhairing by the destruction of hair by breaking the disulphide bonds, which stabilize the hairs. Lime-sulphide immersion method. Hair Root -- The portion of the hair which remains embedded in the skin. Hair-Saving Methods of Unhairing -- Methods of loosening hairs so that they can be easily removed without however tampering with the forces stabilizing their structure. Hair, Shaggy -- Rough and tangled hair. Hair, Sheep -- Some types of sheep grow hair in place of wool. They are indigenous to tropical countries like Brazil, Ethiopia, East, West and South Africa, India, Somalia, South Arabia and Sudan. Leather from skins of such sheep has a finer and tougher grain than from wool bearing sheep. Hair, Short -- See `Ground Hair' Hair Side -- The side of hide or skin with hair on; the grain side. Hair Slip -- Slipping or loosening of the hair in hides and skins due to putrefaction. If the slip is not very bad, passable leather can be made but if advanced too far, the hide is useless to the tanner and can only be made into glue. Badly slipped hides are, therefore, often called `glue' or `glue stock'. Hair, Summer-WInter -- In summer, the hair on cattle hides is shorter and less dense than in winter. In India, hides taken off and cured in winter are, better in quality than those flayed and cured during summer and the hair offers a more or less sure means of distinguishing between summer and winter hides. The dense, long and shiny haired winter hides are preferred to the s~arse, short and dull haired summer stock. ` Hair, White -- The white hair of the cow's body which fetches a better price than black hair. Hand Fleshings -- Removal of flesh by a special type of hand knife from hides and skins. For this, the hide is spread over a beam with the flesh side up. Hand Glazing -- Glazing with a glass slicker by hand. The leather is spread over a table, grain side up and is rubbed with the slicker to get a shine on the leather, Hand Gtwined --- Grain which has been raised or worked up by hand boarding. Handler -- Modern SOICleather tannagc includes three types of liquors, namely, suspender liquors, handler liquors and layers. The handlers or handler liquors are those which follow the suspender liquors. They are stronger than the latter, varying in strength between 15� to 45�Bk, The hides are laid flat in handler liquors. On alternate days, the hides are hauled and piled to allow for the strengthening of the liquors with extracts or stronger tan liquors. These liquors derive their name from this frequent handling. Handling -- Hauling the hides from and laying them down into the liquor of the handler pits. Hand-Hole -- A cut made at the edge of the hide in order to facilitate flaying. Hand Seasoning -� Hand application of seasoning solution with a soft bristle brush or plush pen on leather spread on a table, grain side up. Hand Shaving -- Scraping with a hand shaving knife, the flesh side of tanned leather with a view to making the substance uniform and of desired thickness. Hand Staking -- Mechanical softening of leather by drawing it against a hand stakcr with considerable pressure so as to stretch and open up the fibres. Hide, Brined -- Hide cured by treating with concentrated solution of common salt, or `brining'. In South America the process is largely used for curing hides known as `frigorificos'. Hide, Domestic market. -- Hides obtained from the home

Hides -- In general parlance, the term includes raw, dressed or tanned skins of bullocks, cows, buffaloes, horses, camels, etc, although in statistics and commerce calfskins are also included. Accurately, hides are to be regarded as the outer coverings of large animals in raw or untanned condition. Hides when tanned yield leather. Hides and Skins, Dry-Salted by salt and air dried. -- Hides and skins cured

Hide, Unbathed -- Hide of an animal which was not bathed before slaughter. Hippiness -� Defect noticed in the hides of cows which have had many calves, also defect in hides and skins caused by excrescences of animals. This prevents leather from, lying flat and smooth, in extreme cases its removal leaves holes, breaks the pattern and reduces the cutting value. Hogskin �- The skin of swine; grain grain gloving leather made from the, skins of the peccary and carpincho. The leather is sometimes buffed on the grain and is then known as `Buffed Hogskin' (see also `Carpincho'). Hole -- Accident during flaying, complete perforation of the hide or skin caused by either the knife or the flaying appliance. Hood Hides -- Tanned hides used for making hoods for carriages. Hoof -- The horny protecting substance which grows on the feet of certain animals like horses, cows, etc. Hoof Oil, Bubulum Oil -- See `Oil, Neatsoot'.

Hopea Bark -- The bark of genus of trees Hopes odorota Roxb. fare. Dipterocarpaceae reported to yield supple pale leather. Horn -- A hard projection on the head of certain animals usually bent or curved. Horn Wounds -- The wounds or scars on hides caused by the horns of other animals.

IS 1640:2007 Horny Layer -- The topmost layer of the epidermis consisting of dried epithelial cells. Horse -- A portable wooden vehicle on which leather and skins arc piled for draining or for transporting from one department to another. Horsing Up -- Piling upon the wooden stand known as `horse'. Hose Leather -- Flexible strong leather made from cattle hide, shaved level and so dressed with soft grease as to make it virtually waterproof. Hot Pits -- A set of interconnected circulator pits, usually six in number, in which very strong tan extract liquors of about 130�Bk are used at 40� to 43"C. The leather is suspended in these liquors for a maximum period of one week during which it absorbs the strong cxtroct liquor. Even crude quebracho extract liquor can be employed because of the temperature. Hot pits are used to increase the amount of tannin fixed by the leather to make good the loss sustained in the scouring process and also to fill the butts. The last pit contains only tanning extract liquor and is provided with a closed steam coil for maintaining the temperature at 40�C. By controlling the strength, temperature and pH value of liquors in this pit, these conditions for liquors in other pits are also automatically controlled. Hot pitting is not yet practised in India. Hot Pitting -- Leaving leathers for a certain period in layer pits containing tan liquors of high strength and heated to 33 to 45�C with a view to accelerate the tannin diffusion. Hot Stuffing -- Incorporating grease in the molten condition into leather at a comparatively high temperature. Hue -- Of the three dimensions of colour, hue is the quality recognised as red, blue, etc, as against light, dark or pure/dirty characteristics. Humane Killer -- A lethal weapon used for killing animals (see also `Captive Bolt'). Humectant -- A material, which keeps the surface of the leather moist and thus makes the material flexible. Hump -- Baggy portion of the hide of humped cattle. As Indian cattle are mostly humped, the bulk of the India hides have this baggy pocket on the shoulder. The leather cannot be made to lie quite flat unless cut into two halves or sides. East India kips are, therefore, slit into two sides, called `kip sides' before tanning and finishing. Hyaline Layer (Glassy Layer) --An exceedingly thin film constituting the extreme surface layer of the pelt; if it is damaged, the leather will not take the gloss or polish. It is also called the `glassy layer'. Hyderabads -- Large sized spready variety goatskins, obtainable from Andhra Pradesh. of

Hydraulic Leather -- Leather made from cattle hides used for making pump buckets valves and other purposes. It is vegetable, chrome or combination tanned followed by special stuffing (see also `Gasket Leather'). Hydro Extractor -- Centrifuge machine for removing surplus water from wet leather, also called `whizzer'. Hydrolyzable Tannins -- Vegetable tannins, which are esters of a sugar and a tannic acid and hence on hydrolysis decompose into these components. Hypo Bath -- Second or the reducing bath of the double bath chrome tanning process which contains a solution of sodium thiosulphate or hypo (Na$JO~, 5HZO); also the solution of hypo used for the deposition of sulphur in leather in the sulphur tanning process for making a variety of picking band leather. I Iceland Moss -- Long, fibrous lichen, Cetraria islandica Achar. It produces a mucilage on boiling with water which is used in finishing light leathers made from goat and sheepskins to yield a pliable film on the leather which does not crack on boarding or creasing. It is also sometimes incorporated into casein pigment finishes. Imitation Leather -- Leather like substance much used for upholstering furniture and motor cars, which is very similar to genuine leather in appearance and some properties. Immergan -- Alkyl sulphonyl chloride used as substitute for oil tanning developed in Germany during World War II. Immunization of Hairs -- Stabilization of hairs when exposed to moderate concentrations of alkali in the absence of a reducing agent. The stabilization is attributed to the replacement of disulphide cross-links with more stable ones. Impregnated Bend -- Sole leather bend which has been impregnated with wax, hard grease, rubbery 30

India Rubber -- Caoutchouc, various rubber trees and shrubs. coagulated latex of Industrial Glove -- Glove leathers used for protecting hands of the workers mainly made from chrome splits. In-the-Pearl, Rough, Crust, Blue, White -- Approximately equivalent terms used to describe stock which has been tanned but not finished. `In the-rough' or `rough tanned' is most commonly applied to vegetable tanned cattle hide leather; `in-the-crust' to vegetable and `in-the-white' to alum or formaldehyde tanned sheepskins and lambskins; `in-the-blue' to chrome tanned skins; `in-the-pearl' to chrome tanned stock; `dried-in-the-blue' to crust leather from which white or coloured leather will be made as needed. In-the-Pickle -- Term used to describe skins from which the hair or wool has been removed and which are preserved in a condition ready for tanning, usually in a wet state with salt and acid and sometimes alum. India Tanned -- Term applied to hides and skins tanned in India. This leather is considered as a raw material and is generally `retanned' before finishing. Also called E.I. tanned or East India tanned hides and skins. Indigo Value -- Number of ml of 0.5 percent potassium permanganate solution (w/v) required to neutralize 25 ml Qf indigo s~lution (prepared by treating 5 g of pure indigo-disulphonic acid with 50 g of sulphuric acid and diluting to 1000 ml with water) after dilution with 750 ml of water. lnncs Acid Figures -- When solutions of strong mineral acids are diluted ten times, their pH value is increased by 1.0, whereas weak acids on similar dilution give a figure of only 0.5. Innes had deduced that if a water soluble extract of a leather is diluted tenfold and the resultant increase in its pH value is 0.5, or less, then only a weak acid is present in the water solubles, but if the increase in pH value on tenfold dilution is greater than 0.5, then some strong acid is present.
