Insole Leather -- Hide leather, including flexible splits, vegetable or combination tanned, in sides, bends, shoulders and bellies, suitable for the inner soles of footwear. Inter-fibrillary Substance (Cementing Substance) -- A well defined mass of substance uniformly distributed throughout the dermis of hides and skins composed of gluco-proteins or mucins containing some glucose or sugar in the molecules. It is insoluble in water but is only very slightly soluble in dilute solutions of neutral salts; is digested by alcohol, trypsin and pepsin; and readily dissolved in weak solutions of alkali, such as lime liquor. The bating process helps to make the final leather soft by the removal of this substance from the pelt. Intermediate Coat -- See `Effect Coat'; known as middle coat also. Internal Plasticizer -- A soft polymer used to plasticize a hard polymer (for example, softer acrylics in respect of harder acrylics and polyvinyl acetate in respect of polyvinyl chloride). The advantage is that unlike in external plasticizing, the plasticizing soft polymer does not migrate in course of time, making the film brittle. ( see also `self-plasticized'). Irish Moss -- Dried sea weed of Ireland, and known as Carragheen moss derived from the red algae, Chondvus crispus Lyngb harvested off the Atlantic coast. On boiling the dried moss with water, a gelatinous extract is obtained which is useful as a filler and softening agent in leather finishes (see also `Algin'). Key Test -- A practical test for ascertaining the grain crankiness of leathers. The tip of a key is pressed to the flesh side of leather and drawn with medium force by hand. If there are no cracks observed on the grain side, then the leather passes the test. KHAIR Tree -- Same as `Cutch Tree'. Khari Salt -- Saline earth containing sodium sulphate mixed chiefly with sand and mud used for preserving hides meant for export. A soupy solution of this salt is applied to the flesh side of the hide 5 to 6 times, the hide being dried after each application, yielding a plaster of the muddy salt on the flesh side of the hide, which is often made intentionally thicker to increase the weight. The hides are known in the trade as `drysalted', `khari-salted', `khari s',`nimkis' or `Plastered cured'. If the plaster is thick the cure is called `heavy', otherwise it is called `light'. .-

Leather--A general term for hide or skin with its original fibrous structure more or less intact, tanned to be imputrescible. The hair or wool may or may not have been removed. Leather is also made from a hide or skin which has been split into layers or segmented either before or after tanning, but if the tanned hide or skin is disintegrated mechanically and/or chemically into fibrous particles, small pieces or powders and then, with or without the combination of a binding agent, is made into sheets or other forms, such sheets or forms are not leather. Leguminosae constitutes the logwood of commerce which contains haematoxylin, the colouring principle of logwood. It was originally obtained from the Bay of Campeachy, but it is distributed in Central America and Africa. The species H. campeachianum is cultivated in India. The dye extracted from the wood is used for the production of black colour on leather and fabrics, with the help of iron, chromium and titanium mordants (see also `Haematin' ). Loose Grained -- A grain surface which is not tight and compact (see also `Break of Leather'). Lowenthal Method --A volumetric method of tannin analysis where the tannin is oxidized by potassium permanganate solution, though not very accurate often employed as a routine method in the control of tan liquors. Lower Ends -- The lower grade goods in assortments. Lucknows -- Goatskins coming from Lucknow (Uttar Pradesh) and the neighbourhood, cured partly by wetsalting and partly by dry-salting. Like Kanpurs they are coarse and yield about 4.8 m2 of leather per dozen skins. Lyotropic Agent --Agents, which can sever H-bonds. Both anions and cations have lyotropic effects for example: Cl- and Ca+. The ions have been arranged in Hofmeister series. Lyotropic agents bring about denaturation of proteins and are responsible for permanent swelling in liming of hides and skins. Mangrove Bark -- The term `mangrove' is used in a wide sense for any of the trees that may constitute the vegetation on the tidal mud flats of the tropics and part of the sub-tropics. While mangrove swamps or forests va~ from one part of the world to another, they all have one constant and outstanding feature, namely, the presence of trees of a mangrove family Rhizophoracea especially those belonging to such genera as Rhizophora, Bi'uguicra, Avicennia and Ceriops. A notable feature of the mangrove trees is the richness of the bark in tannin. In India, several varieties of mangrove occur mainly in the Sundarbans in West Bengal. Mangrove Extract -- The name mangrove kutch or `cutch' used for the tanning extract prepared from the mangrove bark is actually a misnomer but being in universal use it is accepted, the name `cutch' being originally used for the extract prepared from heartwood of Acacia catechu. Mangrove `extract' is regarded as the cheapest form of tannin available to the tanner. The average tan content of mangrove extracts (solid) is probably about 65 percent with about 17 percent nontans. The tannin is of the catechol class. It is very soluble and has weight-giving property when used with heavy leather. However, it produces undesirable colour which is very difficult to bleach, and the leather is also inclined to be harsh and thick grained when mangrove is used alone. Mangrove Liquor -- Liquid extract, reddish brown in colour, extremely astringent and yielding a thin, harsh leather. It is a catechol tan, rich in neutral salts but deficient in acid. Marbled Leather -- Variety of fancy leather made usually from sheepskins on which a mottled or marbled effect has been produced by dyeing it in different shades of colour at different places. Marbling -- The process of producing effect on leather. the marbled

The effect is that the grain is damaged and the tensile strength reduced. Masked Tanning -- Tanning with mineral tanning salt masked either with sodium or calcium salts of organic acids developed by Theis et al in 1940s in the U.S. ensures quicker penetration and even distribution of chrome. Mimosa or Wattle Extract -- Tanning extract made from wattle bark. It has a high PH value, a low acid and salt content and a comparatively low viscosity especially in warm solutions. It is largely these attributes that make it suitable for preparing tanning blends suited to almost any purpose. IS 1640:2007 Myrobalans -- Fruits of Terminalia chebula Retz. fare. Combretaceac containing about 30 to 32 percent pyrogallotannin. There are 4 chief market qualities J's (Jubbalpores), V's (Vingolras), B's (Bhimlipatams) and R's (Rajpores). Myrobalan liquor has a bleaching action on Icathcr. Myrobalan Extract -- The solid extract is prepared by extracting the myrobalan nuts of Terminalia chebulu Retz. fare. Combretaceac with water and evaporating the extract. The extract has about 55 percent tannin and 30 percent soluble non-tans. The powdered or spray dried extract has a higher tannin content of about 60 percent. Myrobalan extract liquor deposit insoluble matter, that is, bloom, on standing. It is well suited for blending with other tans and is generally so used. Myrtan -- SeL?`Redunea Extract'. N Nancc Process -- A process of tanning under high vacuum in which the water is expelled from the pores of the pelt at a temperature of 2� to 27�C in the form of vapour thus facilitating quick penetration of tan liquor into the pelt. Nap --Velvety surface of cloth or leather, soft velvety feel of the buffed leather. Nap Finish -- Velvety finish given to the outer surface of leather after the natural grain layer of the leather is removed. Nappa Leather -- Soft, full grain gloving or clothing leather made from unsplit sheep, lamb, and goat or kid skins. It is usually tanned with alum and chromium salts and dyed throughout its substance. In France and Germany also made from side leather for footwear and leather goods purposes. Napalan -- Finished (PU) suede leather. Also written as Nappalan. Nappalan Finish -- Finishing on the flesh side (with or without designs) with a PU finish so that a garment made of such leathers does not require any lining and has the capacity to keep the wearer warm. Native Hides -- Term used to designate American hides from steers, cows or bulls and free of brands. Natural Dyestuffs --Vegetable colouring matters. The most important natural dyestuffs used in the tanning indust~ nowadays are logwood, fistic and perch wood. Nellores -- Hides from Andhra Pradesh State. Some hides are badly branded and of poor quality. Neradol -- Condensation product of formaldehyde 40 with phenol or naphthalene-sulphuric acid used as tanning agent. This was the forerunner of a group of similar substances since prepared and used as synthetic tanning materials. Neutralization -- A process done to offset the acidity or alkalinity of liquor. In connection with chrome leather, it means reduction in the acidity of the freshly chrome tanned leather to avoid troubles in dyeing, fatliquoring and finishing. The acidity is reduced by treating the chrome leather first with a wash in tepid water and subsequently with a weak solution of a weak alkaline reagent. The leather is not rendered neutral, but the pH value of the leather rises to 5.5 to 6.0. Nick -- A notch. Niger -- Goatskin and less commonly sheepskin leather with a natural grain pattern arising from the nature of the skin and the processes and hand working employed, tanned in Nigeria and contiguous districts by primitive methods, usually employing babul pods as the tanning agent. Nigrosine -- Basic azine dyes strongly chelated to iron that the metal cannot bc easily removed. Has deep blue colour very close to black absorption region converting the entire visible range extending into the near IR also. In conjunction with phenolic bodies, they give very deep black colour. Produced as amorphous powder. Soluble in dimethyl formamide, dimethyl sulfoxide, chloroform or equal mixtures of lower alcohols and lower aromatic hydrocarbons. Soluble in pure aromatics or alcohols only in the presence of some fatty acids. Nitrocellulose Finish -- Solutions of specially manufactured nitrated cotton and a resin and plasticizer in a solvent ester usually butyl acetate. The product can be diluted with methylated spirit, toluol or petroleum solvents, and the resulting solution may be sprayed on to the grain surface of the dyed leather and dried to give a waterproof finish. Non-tan -- That part of total solubles, usually sugary matters, gallic acid, soluble mineral salts and other acids which have no tanning property and are not absorbed by the hide powder but give weight and fullness to the leather. Non-tannin -- Same as `Non-Tan'.

North Western -- A variety of cow hides from the area extending from the Himalayas to Bhopal and Allahabad to Saharanpur barring the areas specified under `Agras'. These hides are fairly even in substance and clean as regards the grain but are liable to warbles caused by the bot fly. They are generally air-dried but are sometimes dry-salted, when they are in every way superior to Daccas and Meherpores.

The term is frequently restricted to a pale yellowish brown variety. Offal -- The less valuable parts of a hide such as the heads, shoulders, and bellies. Fagacea containing usually 6 to 9 percent of tannin. Oil Fish -- Drying oil obtained from all parts of different species of the common fish.

IS 1640:2007 Oiling Off -- The process of rubbing oil on the grain side of wet or sammed leather with the object of making the leather soft and in the case of vegetidble tanned leather, preventing the colour of the tannages from darkening by oxidation which it will do if the surface is not protected from direct exposure to air by a thin coat of oil before drying. Practically, all vegetable tanned leathers are oiled off before dyeing, fatliquoring and striking out. A chrome tanned leather is oiled off after dyeing, fat-liquoring and striking out. Oil, Linseed (Flaxseed Oil) -- A yellow to brown oil obtained by expression or solvent extraction of the seeds of the flax plant Linum usitatissimum Linn., fare. Linaceae. Used in the manufacture of paints, varnishes, lacquers and for other purposes. Much used in patent leather manufacture. Oil, Mineral -- Earth Oil, petroleum. for the manufacture of raw hide pickers and also as an oiling and fat-liquoring constituent. Oil, Sulphated -- Product of treatment of vegetable, animal or fish oil with sulphuric acid with subsequent washing and neutralization and used as emulsifier, wetting and softening agent. These oils are also commonly known as sulphonated oils though the term is a chemical misnomer. Oil Tannage -- Process of tanning with animal oils, used in the manufacture of certain soft leathers particularly chamois and certain kinds of buckskin. Generally, fish oils are used for this purpose. Oil Tanning -- A process of tanning involving the incorporation of fish or marine animal oils into prepared skins. These oils are subsequently induced to undergo oxidation and other chemical changes in contact with the skin fibres, leading to chemical combination of oil derivatives with the skin. Oil, Thyme --An essential oil used as an antiseptic in leather finishes. Oil, Turkey Red -- Sulphated castor oil.

Oil, Neatsfoot (Bubulum Oil, Hoof Oil) -- Pale yellow liquid obtained from shin bones and hooves of cattle, used in leather manufacture as a lubricating and waterproofing agent. Much used for fat-liquoring glazed kid after emulsification with soap or after sulphation. Oil Pull-Up -- Two-tone effect observed when a leather is pulled up; the lighter colour at the place of application of force is due to differential distribution of oil caused by the pulling force. Made by brushing suitable non-volatile oil of low viscosity and high refractive index on dyed crust leather followed often by a resin, protein or PU finish. P pH -- Negative logarithm of H+ ion concentration of a solution, Actually pH increases with OH-ion concentration. At pH = O, the H+ concentration is unity and when this concentration is minimum the pH is actually negative. This scale was devised by Sorensen in 1909 and introduced in leather technology in 1911 by Wood and colleagues. pH changes indicate the charge profile of hide/skin/leather and hence very important in the penetration and fixation of charged species by the amphoteric collagen/leather. NeutralpH is 7.0. Below 7.0 is taken as acidic and above 7.0 is taken as alkaline. Otter -- An amphibious animal that frequents rivers and lives on fish. The animal is prized for its short, soft and silky fur. Ounce -- Term used to indicate weight or substance of certain kinds of leather (such as upholstery, bag and case leather). In theory, it is based upon the assumption that one square foot of leather will weigh a certain number of ounces and will uniformly be of a certain thickness; hence a three-ounce leather will theoretically be a leather weighing three ounces per square foot. In practice this varies because of specific gravity of various tanning materials used ~nd for that reason a splitter's gauge has been adopted which controls the commercial thickness of leather when sold by the square foot. An ounce is equivalent to 0.40 mm in thickness. Overflow Liquor -- The vegetable tan liquor that flows out of a system of connected vats when one of the vats is strengthened by the addition of stock liquor. Overflow Vat -- A vat used to receive and store overflow liquor from a series of tanning vats. Over Short Buffer -- Machine equipped with an emery wheel for buffing the flesh side of damp, small skins, as in the making of suede leathers. Oxazolidine -- N and O containing heterocyclic compound used either as a pretanning agent or along with chrome. Leathers pretanned with it can be degreased at higher temperature. When used with chrome it serves to exhaust the bath. 43

Paddle -- A rotating system of radial wooden planks fitted to wooden circular plates at the two ends. The paddle is partly immersed in a pit containing the liquor and stock being processed and provides the much needed agitation when it rotates. Painted Hides -- Hides, the flesh sides of which have been treated with a lime-sulphide mixture. Painting -- The application to the flesh side of raw hides and skins of lime paint which is a mixture of slaked lime, water and sodium sulphide or sodium hydrosulphide. Pancreatic Ferments -- Enzymes, chiefly trypsin, present in the pancreatic juice. The pancreatic ferments

1S 1640:2007 have an efficient bating action on hides and skins and in fact are the constituents of the artificial bates of the trade. Some of these ferments have also been found suitable for unhairing hides. Pancrcatin -- Enzymes chiefly trypsin obtained from the pancreas of an animal. Pan Scale -- Calcium sulphate from brine crystallization used in cattle feed and as a fertilizer. Paperiness -- Emptiness of leather due to less filling up or due to lack of substance. Parcel (Raw Skins) -- 500 pieces weighing ordinarily 150 to 160 kg approximately, but may go up to lots of 450 kg. Parchment -- Translucent or opaque skin material with a smooth surface suitable for writing, bookbinding and other purposes. It is made from thin skins of sheep, goat, calf, pig or ass, by drying out the limed material without applying any tannage, the material being thoroughly cleansed, degrcazed and smoothened
during the process.

Pasting (Paste Drying) -- Drying damp leather in a stretched out condition by pasting leather, with the flesh side up, with an adhesive to a smooth glass or enamelled plate. Pasting imparts to leather a smooth grain surface and a larger area than drying by toggling or nailing. Patent Finish -- Glossy finish made with cooked (by boiling) linseed oil applied in three coats -- the daub (0.002 5" thick), the brush coat (0.002 S" thick) and the varnish coat (0.005" thick). Naphtha was used to thin the varnish. Pigments/Metallic powders were also incorporated in the daub coat. Film formation is by the oxidation of the liquid varnish into a solid film. The finish is alternatively known as `Japanning' or `Enameling'. The advent of PU finishes for making patent leathers has relegated this classical finish to background. The thickness of PU patent finish films is in the range of 100 to 120 m. Patent Leather -- Leather with a lustrous mirror-like surface, built up by the application of one or more coats of daubs, varnishes or lacquers pigmented or nonpigmented, based on linseed oil, nitrocellulose, polyurethane aucb'or other synthetic resins. In certain countries laminates of a similar appearance may be classed as patent leather, but different countries limit the proportion or thickness of the plastic film in different ways. Patent Plastic -- See `Plastic Patent'.

Penetration Time -- Duration of flexing in minutes which is just suficient to cause water to penetrate from the wetted (grain) surface to the other face of the material. Pepper Box -- The pattern produced on grain surface of leather from grubby hides which often resembles buck-shot marks. Percentage Basicity -- The number of hydroxyl groups borne by a chromium unit as a percentage fraction of the same present in chromic hydroxide. Perch -- Equipment used in light leather tanneries which consists of an overhead horizontal beam mounted on to `A'-shaped legs and having a groove along the centre of the beam. There is another circular wooden rod which can be lifted or lowered to fit in the grove. Crust skin is clamped in the groove of the perch by means of the rod which is secured by a special clamp at one end of the perch. The skin is thus securely fixed on the perch and hangs down and its flesh side is worked with a moon knife which softens the skin without raising any grain on the grain side. 44

Pickled Skins --- Skins for export, usually unhaired, packed in barrels or casks with a saturated brine solution sometimes mixed with alum. Pickling -� The treatment of scudded and bated skins or drenched skins with a solution of salt and acid, such as sulphuric, hydrochloric, formic, etc, to preserve thcm or as a preparation for the tanning operation so as to prevent drawn grain. Pickling brings the pelt into a non-swollen acid condition which is very necessary as a preliminary to the one-bath chrome tannage. Comnlonly used before chrome tanning but not, generally, in vegetable tanning. Pickling also preserves limed and delimed pelt in a sound condition and enables them to be exported in wooden casks. pigment (Colouring Matter) -- A finely ground opaque coloured material insoluble in water often adclcd to leather finishes to provide colour and to mask defects in the grain surface of the leather. Phosphate Oils -- Made by trans-esterification of an oil with phosphoric acid to replace some of the fatty acids of the oil. The chief advantages of these are: a) They can react with collagen as well as mineral tanning agents like chromium and alurninium. Being reactive lubricants thus, the desired degree of lubrication can be had with lesser amount of phosphate oil. They can hold four times more raw oil than sulphited/sulphated oils and hence can impart greater fulliless to leather. Moreover, they- can act as fire-retardants too.

Post Mortem Changes -- Chemical and structural changes that naturally occur, in a hide between the time of slaughter and that of the curing or other preservative operations. Pound -- A unit of measurement. For dry or drysalted hides, a hide pound is equivalent to 20 ordinary pounds. But for wet-salted hides a 16 pound is used as the unit. Pressing -- Removing the bulk of water from wet leather by means of a hydraulic press. Press Leach System -- System of extracting tannins from vegetable tanstuffs in which the liquor passes from pit to pit round the battery by virtue of its own weight and a constantly increasing specific gravity. Press Over System -- A system of working circular pits in a series which ensures a uniformly gradual decrease in the strength of liquors in the pits of the battery. The strong liquor from the leach vat or the extract vat is pumped into the head circulator. This causes a successive movement of liquors from one pit to the next one, pushing the comparatively stronger liquor of any one pit into the weaker liquor of the next pit. The weakest liquor then flows out from the tail circular pit into the drain. Pre-tanning -- Preliminary tanning carried out prior to main tanning with the intension of avoiding casehardening and for acceleration of tanning, 46

Pitted Leather -- Leather with holes larger than pinholes caused by bacterial action on leaving the skins too long in the soak pits in warm weather. Plastered Kips -- Dry-salted kips.

Plastic Patent -- A material made from vinyl resins or other materials to resemble patent leather. According to the US Federal Trade Commission ruling, the use of term `Plastic patent leather' is incorrect. Plasticizer --A material added to a solution or mixture for the purpose of softening (or rendering plastic) the film obtained on drying the mixture. Cellulose lacquer solutions invariably dry to form harsh or brittle films on leather but if mixed with a plasticizer, the film becomes pliable and non-cracky. Plasticizers have generally high boiling points and hence they remain in the film, ensuring plasticity. These are generally high boiling liquids like tricresyl phosphate, diamyl tartrate, ethyl citrate and others. Sulphated oils can be used as plasticizers in aqueous leather finishes.

Puer -- Infusion of dog dung used for bating. Puering -- Treating the fleshed limed pelts or grains with a warm infusion of dog dung for 1.5 to 5 hours according to the type of pelt in order to remove traces ofepithelial tissue, short hair, lime soaps and cementing substance, loosen the scud, deplete the pelts, complete the deliming and increase the stretch and pliability of the finished leather. Quebracho Wood Extract --The solid extract is dark brownish-black and contains 62 to 63 percent tannins and 7 to 8 percent of non-tannins. As a tanning material, it belongs to the catechol class. There are two forms of the extract, the ordinary or untreated extract, not very soluble in cold water and the sulphited or cold water soluble extract. IS 1640:2007 percent of sodium bisulphate. Warm crude qucbracho liquors arc used in the filling of heavy leather in the final stages of manufacture in order to produce tlrmness, solidity and wear. Range, Butt or Bend -- In respect of sole leather, a butt or bend range is a strip of sole leather of convenient width cut from a butt or bend at right angles to the back bone. Raw Hide for Mechanical Use -- Cattle hide that has been dehaired and limed, often stuffed with oil and grease, and has sometimes undergone other preparatory processes but has not been tanned. Raw hide is used principally for mechanical purposes for belt lacings and pins, loom pickers, gaskets, pinions and gears. Some raw hide is dressed with hair left on. Raw Hide Belting Leather -- Semi-tanned cattle hide leather suitable for manufacture of high speed machine belting. Raw Hide Lace -- Buffalo hide, limed, dehaired, dried out and lightly oiled. Raw Hide for Luggage -- Translucent material made from the grain side of cattle hides freed from hair and the flesh layer, and dried out in the limed state usually without any tanning process being applied. Red Heat -- Coloration usually red, which appears on the flesh side of salted raw hides and skins. The stains do not generally damage the hide or skin. The organisms responsible for red heat are not found on the raw hides or skins but are introduced through the use of certain marine salts. Two, types of bacteria have been isolated; a redsarcina and a yellow one, belonging to the sub-genus of the genus sarcina fare. Micrococceae. Red sarcina is non-proteolytic but the yellow one is proteolytic and can liquefy gelatin. 48

Radiation Curing -- Insolubilizing finish films (formed of aqueous dispersions) using radiation, either UV or Electron beam. The insolubilization is effected by cross-linking brought about by free radicals induced by radiation. The cross-linking chemicals to be incorporated for the purpose are: Formaldehyde, aziridine epoxides and carbo-di-imides. Though crosslinking PU finishes only have been achieved satisfactorily, it is likely to be extended to acrylics also in the near future. The importance of radiation curing arises from the fact that all finishes are required to be all-water-soluble systems to avoid air pollution from the use of solvent-based lacquers. Rendering -- Separating fats from protein connective tissue and other water insoluble substances by treating small pieces of animal matter with hot water or steam. Reptile Skins -- Skins of the class of animals comprising snakes, lizards, turtles, crocodiles, etc. Resilience of Leather -- It is measured by percentage rebound of a standard plunger dropped onto the leather surface under standard conditions. Resin Dispersion -- Aqueous dispersions of methacrylate and other acrylate resins have a milky appearance and acid reaction and can be diluted with water or mixed with aqueous dispersions of casein, pigment finishes, binders, etc. Commercial dispersions contain from 30 to 40 percent of a highly polymerized acrylate resin. As the resin is thermoplastic, the finishes when dry on the leather cannot be glazed by the glazing machine or ironed by hot iron and they are usually hot plated by a leather press. These resin dispersions were first used as an undercoat for nitrocellulosc finishes in the manufacture of upholstery leather to prevent the migration of the plasticizer from the nitrocellulose tilm into the leather and thus making the nitrocellulosc film brittle. It has also been used along with aqueous pigment dispersions for application to well snuffed or corrected leather grains and also in mixtures with water pigment dispersions, which are then applied to leather, dried, and rendered fast to wet rubbing by the application of a colorless, nitrocellulosc lacquer top coat. Roller Basil -- Leather with a smooth finish, a specially fine grain and a compact firm structure commonly natural coloured but sometimes dyed red, made from hill sheep, vegetable tanned and designed to bc suitable for covering the drawing rollers of cotton spinning machinery and for other purposes, such as book binding for account books. Roller Coater -- The same as those used in printing industry, both direct and offset; adopted by leather industry in 1960's; useful for simple application of finishes, tipping of embossed leathers and printing fashion designs. The first area in which roller coater was used was in split Icather finishing. Roller Leather -- Leather made from sheepskins tanned by vegetable process and finished so as to have a smooth and plain grain and even substance. This leather is much used for rollers of cotton spinning machinery. 50

Rounding -- The operation of cutting off the offal, that is, the bellies and the shoulder, from the substantial portion of a hide, namely, the butt. It is usually done after the hides have been unhaired by liming. Only the hides meant for the manufacture of heavy leathers like sole, belting or picking bands are rounded. The butts arc given a superior tannage and the offals go through a cheaper tanning process. Rounding Machine from the butt. -- Machine for cutting the offal

Round Spots -- Rings of a thickness of 2 to 3 mm and an outside diameter of 1 cm, appearing after removal of the hair. Rub Fastness -- The fastness of finish to rubbing, both dry and wet, The leather is rubbed with a felt pad either dry or wet attached to a fastness tester. The rubbed surface of the leather is compared with spots of five different degrees of greyness constituting a Grey scale, marked 1 to 5, in the increasing order of rub fastness. Scratch Resistance -- Resistance of a finish to direct scratching with a sharp instrument expressed as kilograms/mm square of the width of the scratch. Screen Printing -- Colouring the leather surface through a screen, which has a stenciled design and fixing the colour. For every colour, a separate screen is necessary. Scud -- A slimy material containing the natural dirt of hides and skins; remnants of epithelial tissue, hair pigment, lime soap, etc, left in the grain layer. Scudding -- Removing the scud from unhaired hides and skins by the scraping action of a knife or blade by hand or by machine.

IS 1640:2007 Semi-chrome -- Leather tanned first with vegetable tannin and then with chrome salts. Sequestering Agents -- Compounds which are capable of forming complexes with metals and are useful for the prevention of undesirable effects due to metals. Thus leathers which have been treated with certain meta-phosphates are immune against the catalytic effects of iron compounds. Shake Tare -- Weight taken after shaking the hides free from loose salts. Shaking -- Sweeping and beating wet-salted hides against a piece of stone or stump of wood to free them from the loose salt before weighing. Shanks -- That portion of the hide which covers the leg of an animal. Sharkskin -- Genuine sharkskin leather is made from the top grain of skins of certain species of sharks and is used principally in shoes, belts, wrist-watch straps, luggage, fine leather goods and for industrial purposes. It has varying natural grain markings of tine, smooth, mesh-like grain similar to pin seal. The term is wrongly applied to other leathers, such as horse butts embossed with a shark grain. Sodium Trichlorophenate -- A water soluble liquid preservative. It gives excellent results against moulds, fungi and bacteria. Sod Oil -- In England, the type of fish oil used for chamoising does not remain after oxidation, in a sufficiently liquid condition to be pressed out, as in the case of moellon degras used on the continent of Europe. In England, the chamois leather, after the oxidation of the fish oil, is washed with washing soda or sodium carbonate whereby the oxidized fish oil is removed from the chamois leather partly in an emulsified form and partly in the form of soap. The alkaline wash water is then treated with sulphuric acid when the fish oil is separated from the soap and from the emulsion. This separated oxidized fish oil is known as sod oil and has properties of moellon degras and is used for similar purposes (see also `Moellon Degras'). -- Leather used for soles of boots and

IS 1640:2007 shoes. Sole leather is generally made from thick hides, such as those of buffalo or ox. Generally, sole leather is vegetable tanned; chrome tanned sole leather has very limited use. Solid Leather -- Designates an article the body of which is made of leather. If the term `solid' is prefixed to the name of the particular skin, for example, solid pigskin, it indicates that the article is made essentially of a single thickness of leather of the kind specified. Solubilized Extracts -- Several tanning materials, such as quebracho, hemlock, etc, contain large quantities of sparingly soluble tannins, which can be rendered soluble by treatment with alkali sulphites or bisulphites. Extracts thus prepared are called solubilized extracts. Solvent Dyeing -- Dyeing in an organic solvent nmdiutn. The tncthod is useful for water insoluble dyes. The colour of the dyed leather is fast to washing. Solvent Fatliquoring -- Fatliquoring with an emulsion of water in oil dissolved in a solvent like kerosene. Solvent Resistance -- Resistance to organic solvent extraction; very much desirable in respect of garment leathers as they are subjected frequently to dry cleaning. Sonagaddi -- See `Lizardskins'. Spew -- White crystalline or gummy deposit appearing on grain surface of finished leather on ageing. It may be caused by the crystallization of salts in leather or by the appearance on the leather surface of fatty acids present in the leather. Even if spew is removed by wiping the leather, it reappears continuously. Its presence in finished leather is a great defect. Spew Fatty -- Spew caused by excessive fat. Split -- The under layer of a hide or skin or part of a hide or skin separated by splitting. If the name of the animal whence it originates, or the word `hide' or `skin' or the part of the animal whence it comes is included in the description, then the word `split' must be used as a noun, for example, pig split, hide split, butt split and not as an adjective, for example, split pigskin. Split Finishing -- Finishing the flesh splits. Involves scaling the split surface either with a soft polymer which can get into the pores of the split leather and can have good anchorage and then finishing the surface with resin binder, etc., or by laminating the split leather with a thick PU foil. The importance of split finishing lies in the worldwide shortage of hides and skins. Splitting -- Dividing or cutting leather, hides and skins into thin pieces along a horizontal plane, Cutting a hide vertically with a knife into sides, bends, bellies, etc, is also called splitting. Split Hides -- The outer or grain layer of a hide from which the under or flesh side has been split to give it a reasonably uniform thickness. Split Skins -- Skins which have been split into two parallels with the grain or flesh surface. The term is used to describe the portion of a hide or skin split into two or more thicknesses other than the grain or hair side. Spue -- Same as `Spew'. Stage Hide -- The hide of a male of the ox kind that was castrated later in life than the steer, often when a year old. The longer the castration is delayed, the more the hide becomes like a bull's. It has no recognized designation in the hide market, but is classed as steer or bull whichever it resembles more closely, causing frequent difficulties in classification. Stratum Corneum -- The uppermost layer of the epidermis made up of dried hardened and flattened cells which is shed as scurf. Stratum Granulosum -- The third layer of the epidermis from the surface and containing keratohyaline granules. Stratum Lucidum -- The layer of the epidermis in between stratum corneum and stratum granulosum. Stratum Rete Mucosum or Stratum Germinativum -- The lowest layer of epidermis containing germinating cells, It is in immediate contact with derma, and constitutes the chief and most important layer of the epidermis. The cells of this layer are at all times reproducing new cells. Stretched Bamboo Hides -- See `Firrnas'.

Suede Splits -- Leather made from the flesh splits of hides or skins and finished with a velvet like nap. Sulphated Oils -- Self-emulsifying oils. The Sulphato (OS03H) groups linked to the carbon of the oil through a mediating `O' are the emulsifier part. The emulsifying group can split off in the presence of acids and hence is not acid-stable. Sulphited Oil -- Self-emulsifying oils, carrying the sulphonic acid groups -- SO~H as the emulsifying part. Since in this group the sulphur atom is directly attached to carbon of the oil, the anionic fatliquors made thereof are resistant to both acid and salt and hence can be introduced along with pickle itself to prevent sticking together of the separated fibrcs; can hold more neutral oil; their increased molecular size enables them to lubricate better and produce smoother and softer chrome leathers; when used in very large amounts make Icather heavy and looser. IS 1640:2007 fairly widely distributed in North West India and both the leaves and barks are much used locally as a tanning material. The average tannin content of the bark is 16 percent (dry material) which varies seasonally (that collected during the rainy season had the highest tan content). Leaves collected in autumn had the highest tan content (21 -26 percent). It has, however, not been commercially exploited for export. Sunmac Extract -- Liquid extract made from sumac, by the use of water at 50; to 60"C. Boiling water is not used, as it destroys the tannins present. Half an hour boiling destroys at least 25 percent of the tannin. Sumac Liquor -- Sumac infusion. Liquors in general made from sumac are liable to vary in composition, more so than most tanning materials. Sumac has in general a higher pH value than other materials and a the grain layer near consisting of water, mineral matter and passed out from the the hair bulbs and secrete sweat together with a little urea and other waste products which are body through the skin pores.

Sweating Room -- A warm, closed room saturated with moisture used for hanging hides and skins for loosening the hair or wool by bacterial action. Swelling -- When hides and skins are immersed in an alkaline or acid solution, for example, in lime liquor or sour tan liquor, they swell causing an increase in their thickness and weight. Sweating -- Loosening the hair or wool by hanging the hides or skins in a closed atmosphere saturated with moisture thus encouraging bacterial action. The bacteria attack the roots of the hair or wool which is then easily removed. Sheepskins are generally hung in damp, underground chambers at 10� to 15�C in cold sweating and 20� to 25� C in warm sweating, for 48 hours. This deposition is effected by treating the hides or skins first in a strong solution of hypo and subsequently in a solution of either sulphuric or hydrochloric acid and salt. By the action of the acid on the hypo already absorbed by the hide, sulphur is deposited on the fibres which produce a mild tannage. Sulphur tannage is also used in the combination process oftannage of picking band Ieathcr in which heavy hides are first sulphur tanned and then oil tanned and finally vegetable tanned. Terais -- Cow hides obtainable from areas around the foot of the Himalayas including Nepal. Air-dried, large in size, running very even up to the shoulder and producing a compact leather. Teri Pod ---Pods or fruits of Caesalpinia di~na Rottl., fare. Leguminosae. The tannin content of the husk (dry pods freed of seeds) has been found to be 52 percent. Ticks (Cattle) -- Arthropod parasites of the order Acarina infesting verte-brate animals which lodge on the body of cattle and suck the blood causing small punctures or wounds. Trade Organizations (Raw Hides and Skins), AI1Round Sale -- Many tanners and exporters have their purchasing agents in the districts for raw hides and skins but ordinarily, hides and skins pass through the hands of various middlemen. Eventually, they find their way to aarhutdo~ a godown keeper, who residing at the larger ccntres acts as a commission agent between the bepari and the dealer and the tanner or the exporter. Parcels of hides dispatched to the acwhatdar may contain anything from 100 to 10 000 pieces. The aarlratdar usually advances from 75 to 80 pcrccnt of the market value ofthc hides to the bepari immediately on receiving the railway receipt and when the competition is keen even more. The bqxwi ordinarily fixes a minimum selling price for the hides. The aat-hatdur makes a rough selection of the hide for his own purposes and then usually sells them `all-round' or `over-all' that is to say the purchaser accepts a parcel of hides containing all grades and is not permitted to select merely the best. An `all-round' parcel might contain for instance 30 percent slaughtered, 45 percent deads, and25 percent rejections and doubles. An overall parcel of 10000 hides might produce as many as 70 selections for export baling. Even in `all-round' lot, a rebate is sometimes claimed on the ground that the whole batch has not come LIp to an examined sample, usually of fifty. The aarhatdar's sale is a private auction, bids of each firm being ordinarily kept secret. The aarhatdar receives a commission on the number of hides sold. This commission was formerly about Rs 1.50 to Rs. 2.00 for each 20 hides. The hides arc actually sold by weight. The shipper carefully assorts them for export although the actual work is done largely by poorly paid labour. The classification is ordinarily done before the hides leave the aarhatdar's godown but the selection is checked again in the shipper's godown. There they are trimmed and baled. Tragacanth (Gum Tragacanth, Bassora Gum, Goat's Thorn) -- An exudation from Astragalus gummzyer Labill., fare. Lcguminosae used in leather dressing. Transfer Foil -- The entire finish film (i.e. all the three layers in the reverse order) formed on a supporting polythcne film. When this is transferred onto a leather, polythene supporter side up, by pressing it onto the 61 leather and then peeling off the supporter film, the leather gets a finished appearance in one operation. This is an elegant material for pollution -- free finishing. Tray Dyeing -- The method used for dyeing light skins only. The moist skins are either folded or paired together flesh to flesh and dipped in warm dyestuff solution in the tray until the desired depth of shade is obtained. Trim -- Production of a good pattern by cutting the edges of hides neatly, evenly and symmetrically and by separating the parts which are not useful to tanners, such as heads, shanks, tails, etc. Trimmings -- The small pieces cut from the edge in trimming the hides and used for making glue. Trimming Shearing -- Tanned and dressed sheep or lambskin with short to medium, length wool suitable for trimming purposes. Upper Leather -- Leather for making upper part of boots and shoes usually manufactured from calfskins, goatskins, cattle hides or horse hides.

v
Vache Sole Leather -- Sole made from ox hide.

Vachette �- Literally the hide of heifer. The French equivalent of `kip' or more often of `kip leather'. Vacuum Drying -- Drying with heat and pressure reduced by about 28" to 29" of mercury, enough to make water boil at 12 to 18�C and a temperature of 140 to 200"F on the hot plate. Greater area yield, better streamlining production flow and better suitability to 62

grain leathers than paste drying, similarly shorter duration of drying and tight break are some distinct advantages. Disadvantages are loss in thickness, requiring more uniform neutralisation throughout the thickness and migration of dyes and neutral oils. More of neutral oil has to be used to compensate for the loss due to migration and to prevent the consequent dry feel. Sulphated oils are better than sulfonated oils for use in leathers to be dried by the vacuum drying method. Of the two variations, Straight Through and Vacuum Crusting, the latter is better. Vacuum drying is the third major method of drying, introduced around 1962. Originally designed for fill drying, it is now used for partial drying to set the grain to be followed by a slower air-drying.

Bureau of Indian Standards BIS is a statutory institution established under the Bureau harmonious development of the activities of standardization, and attending to connected matters in the country. Copyright BIS has the copyright of aIl its publications. No part of these publications may be reproduced in any form without the prior permission in writing of BIS. This does not preclude the free use, in the course of implementing the standard, of necessary details, such as symbols and sizes, type or grade designations. Enquiries relating to copyright be addressed to the Director (Publications), BIS. Review of Indian Standards of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote marking and quality certification of goods

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are

needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards
should ascertain that they are in possession of the }atest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of

`BIS Catalogue' and `Standards : Monthly Additions'. This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc : No. CHD 17 (868).
